1.title: Chest Pain
1.chiefComplaint: Chest pain with severe respiratory distress
1.caseSummary:
Differential: Aortic dissection, Tension pneumothorax, Asthma exacerbation, Pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, Angina.

The patient has a tension pneumothorax. This is a medical emergency. No time should be wasted in this case. The tension pneumothorax should be diagnosed through the physical exam and not through radiology. A
thoracentesis is a good diagnostic procedure to confirm your physical exam findings of a tension pneumothorax. This is a short term fix and a chest tube should be placed. After a chest tube is placed, it is important to get an
X-ray to confirm the correct placement of the chest tube. After the chest tube is in place and the placement is confirmed, the patient should be transferred to the ward for monitoring,

2.title: Altered Mental Status
2.caseSummary:
Differential: The differential for altered mental status in an elderly patient includes: seizures, bacterial meningitis, urinary tract infection, trauma, electrolyte disturbances, drug or alcohol toxicity, heart failure, metabolic

disorders (hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia, uremia, liver failure, thyrotoxicosis).

The patient has a subdural hematoma. The clue is that the patient had a recent fall and has been having episodes of altered mental status since that time. The patient is also at a higher risk for subdural hematomas due to his
advanced age and being a chronic alcoholic. Especially with falls in the elderly, it is important to check for head trauma. CT Without contrast is more widely used for the swift turn-around time for results, but MRI is more
sensitive in detecting intracranial hemorrhages. Time is of utmost importance in this case as bleeds may cause mass effects that may lead to increased brain damage as time overlaps. Neurosurgery should be consulted to
evacuate the subdural hematoma. Once neurosurgery is consulted, the case will end.

Subdural hematomas are a result from venous bleeding after blunt head trauma. The movement of the brain relative to the skull causes rupture of the bridging veins. Risks factors as noted above include: advanced age,

alcoholics, and patients undergoing anticoagulation.

3.title: Pelvic Pain
3.chiefComplaint: Severe pelvic pain, worse with intercourse
3.caseSummary:
e. Correct locations at this time were: Inpatient Unit

Differential: There is a large differential for a right adnexal mass in a reproductive age female. This could include ectopic pregnancy, tuboovarian abscess, inflammatory bowel disease, ovarian mass, endometrioma, theca

lutein cysts, germ cell neoplasms, metastatic diseases, and many others.

The patient has an endometrioma, She is having severe pelvic pain which worsens with sexual activity. Typically a pelvic ultrasound is performed, but a CT scan or a MRI of the abdomen/pelvis area would also be acceptable
to find the endometrioma. This can be removed by ordering a laparotomy. It is also acceptable to consult OB/GYN who can do the laparotomy. Once this is done, the case will end. You can then do preventative measures of

counseling regarding smoking cessation and illicit drug use.

5.title: Headache
5.caseSummary:
Differential: Broad differential but includes: Stroke (likely cerebellar stroke), bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, sepsis, intracranial abscess, Herpes Simplex |, head trauma, Multiple Sclerosis, Tumor.

The patient has West Nile Encephalitis. This is a difficult case, and it is only testing your diagnostic skills. There is little treatment involved in this case. The patient is experiencing neurological symptoms, so a neurological
infection, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage and tumor should be high on your differential. A CT/MRI could help differentiate these causes. The patient then should have a lumbar puncture performed and CSF should be sent
out to test for protein, glucose, and cell count. With normal glucose, elevated lymphocyte count, and increased levels of protein, this suggests a viral meningeal infection. It is still a good idea to send out CSF cultures for

fungal, viral, and bacterial pathogens. Note that the West Nile Virus can show up negative in a CSF viral culture. Once you test for the West Nile Virus antibody and it shows up positive, the case will end. In your last two
minutes, you can perform/schedule preventive measures that the patient needs — a pap smear, mammogram, and the Tdap vaccine.

6.caseSummary:
Differential: Differential for this patient could include Mononucleosis, cytomegalovirus, acute HIV infection, Strep throat, Toxoplasma gondii, and other viral infections

This patient has mononucleosis, and this can be diagnosed by history and physical exam and confirmed by an infectious mononucleosis screening test. It is characterized by a sore throat often with palatal petechiae, fever,
malaise, posterior cervical adenopathy and splenomegaly. If the patient were older, it would be important to warn the family that the patient should avoid contact sports to prevent splenic rupture during the course of the
illness. However, as the patient is only 6 years old, this is not a required order.
6.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old child who presents with fever, sore throat, malaise, and generalized rash. Exam reveals posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, palatal petechiae, and splenomegaly. The combination of pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, fever, and the characteristic maculopapular rash is classic for infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The differential includes other viral infections (CMV, acute HIV), streptococcal pharyngitis, and toxoplasmosis. Key management considerations: avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes characteristic EBV rash), avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome risk in febrile children), and in older patients, restrict contact sports to prevent splenic rupture.

7.title: Generalized Weakness
7.caseSummary:
Differential: This case is a classic presentation of myasthenia gravis. However, other things that should be in your differential are: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy,
and motor neuron disease.

The prevalence of Myasthenia Gravis is 1 in 7500. The cause of myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune antibody against the acetylcholine receptor which is causes skeletal muscle weakness with preservation of sensation and
reflexes. The likelihood of having a positive antibody against the acetylcholine receptor is about 80% (50% if it only involves the ocular muscles). Weakness is exacerbated by continued use of the muscle and improved by rest.
The kind of muscles involved can vary but can included extraocular muscles (causing blurry vision), eyelids (causing ptosis), facial muscles (causing difficulty in chewing and slurred speech). Myasthenia Gravis can also cause
limb muscle weakness (proximal and asymmetric). Generally, the classic symptoms are: ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Electromyography (EMG) can confirm the diagnosis - repetitive stimulation would demonstrate a
decreased signal strength. This can differentiate Myasthenia gravis from Lambert-Eaton, should would show the opposite - an increased neuromuscular signal with repetitive stimulation.

The CT shows a thymoma which occurs in 15% of the patients. It is essential to remove a thymoma as this leads to improvement in symptoms and outcome in about 85% of patients. Treatment would include
anticholinesterase medications such as pyridostigmine. Immunosuppressives are also mainstay treatments as Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition. Prednisone, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine are all
treatments. If the patient is still not improving, plasmapheresis can be done to remove antibodies against the acetylcholine receptors. If plasmapheresis is ineffective, IVIG can also be used as a treatment.

A question arises as to why you do not just use pytidostigmine as monotherapy. This patient is having respiratory symptoms and has a low oxygen level on presentation. Pyridostigmine does not treat the underlying disease
and only helps with symptoms. Also, pyridostigmine will cause a cholinergic effect and increase airway secretions which may worsen any pulmonary complications. Therefore, you should use pyridostigmine in conjunction
with something that treats the underlying disease such as steroids or azathioprine. Using pyridostigmine as monotherapy might be appropriate for mild cases of myasthenia gravis where the patient has mild symptoms of
ptosis, fatigue, or muscle weakness. However, once the respiratory system becomes involved, it should be treated aggressively and monitored closely to prevent respiratory distress.

She has developed ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Respiratory muscle involvement is present with mild hypoxemia from hypoventilation. Exam reveals fatigable weakness with preservation of sensation and reflexes — the hallmark of myasthenia gravis. The underlying pathophysiology is autoimmune antibody-mediated destruction of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. CT chest is essential to evaluate for thymoma, which is present in 10-15% of MG patients and whose resection can lead to remission in ~85%.

8.title: Burning During Urination
8.caseSummary:
Differential: Cystitis, urethritis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis.

This 19-year-old patient is presenting with dysuria with fevers and chills. The differential mentioned above should come to mind. The patient is sexually active, so sexually transmitted infections should be considered as a
cause of his presenting symptoms. The first step is to get an UA, a gram stain, and a urine culture. No blood culture is necessary because the patient does not meet criteria for SIRS. Presence of typical symptoms such as
‘edema and tendermess of the prostate on physical exam is enough to confirm the diagnosis. In normal practice, care should be used to not do a vigorous prostate massage because this can increase the risk for bacteremia.
Delaying antimicrobial therapy can increase the risk of complications of bacteremia and abscesses. Fluoroquinolones are the treatment of choice because it can penetrate inflamed prostate. Ciprofloxacin x 14-28 days would
be a good choice. However, Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can also be used. In this case, the offending agent is E-coli. E-coli accounts for about a 1/3 of the infections for prostatitis. Other bacteria include: enterococci,
pseudomonas, and S. epidermidis.

Chlamydia and gonorrhea tests should be performed to rule out a sexually transmitted infection,
If the patient had CVA tenderness (suggesting pyelonephritis), then you would use a fluoroquinolone, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, or an oral cephalosporin as an outpatient. As an inpatient, ceftriaxone IV can be used. In
patients with pyelonephritis, if being adequately treated by antibiotics for 72 hours and still not improving, a CT scan of the abdomen should be done to rule out a renal abscess.

If this weren't the first urinary infection in this patient, an urologic workup should be complete which includes a renal ultrasound, a CT of the abdomen, and a voiding cystography.

9.title: Abdominal Pain
9.chiefComplaint: RLQ abdominal pain, fever, nausea post-appendectomy
9.caseSummary:
Differential: Abdominal pain has a broad differential. However, the pain is somewhat localizing to the RLQ. This would suggest that the differential includes Abdominal abscess, kidney stone, Pelvic inflammatory disease,

Abdominal wall pain, and ectopic pregnancy.

With this patient's recent appendectomy and symptoms of RLQ abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis, this is highly suggestive of an intra-abdominal abscess.
Percutaneous abscess drainage is preferred as it avoids a possibly difficult laparotomy, the requirement of anesthesia, avoids wound complications associated with intra-abdominal surgery, and reduces length of

hospitalization.

This can be performed if there are no signs of necrotic tissue and the area is within reach of percutaneous drainage. Empiric antibiotic coverage should cover gram-negative organisms, anaerobes, and enterococci. Gram-stain

of the abscess can provide early guidance for selection of antibiotics.
9.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a young woman with recent appendectomy who presents to the inpatient unit with RLQ abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia, nausea, and vomiting. She is febrile and tachycardic with localized RLQ tenderness. Labs show leukocytosis. The combination of recent abdominal surgery, fever, tachycardia, and localized pain is highly suggestive of a postoperative intra-abdominal abscess. CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast is the imaging of choice. Management involves percutaneous image-guided abscess drainage (first-line, avoiding the morbidity of open laparotomy) plus broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics covering gram-negative organisms, anaerobes, and enterococci.

10.title: Pain in Legs
10.chiefComplaint: Bilateral leg pain on exertion, relieved by rest
10.caseSummary:
Differential: Peripheral vascular disease, Coagulopathy, spinal claudication, sciatica, embolism, Thromboangiitis obliterans.
Peripheral Artery disease can be remembered by the 6 P’s - Pulselessness, pain, pallor, poikilothermia, paresthesia, and paralysis. The patient has many risk factors associated with peripheral vascular disease: hypertension,
hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and smoking. Since the patient is experiencing intermittent claudication and not rest pain, the treatment is conservative. The main way to diagnose the patient is through ABI and pulse volume
recordings.

Normal ABI >= 1.0, Claudication ABI <0.7, Rest pain ABI < 0.4.

Arteriography would cause you to lose points on this case because this is an invasive test, and the patient should first be tried on conservative treatment. Conservative treatment is namely: controlling the patient's
hypertension, encouraging the patient to lose weight, smoking cessation, controlling cholesterol, and controlling blood sugars. If the patient had rest pain, the patient could be a considered for vascular surgery (surgical
bypass grafting or angioplasty).

The patient should be started on an antihypertensive agent, but lisinopril or other ACEI would be the drug of choice due to the patient having elevated glucose levels, and this would be protective for the kidney. Also, the
patient should be started on a statin as well as 2 glucose lowering agent such as metformin. The patient will checkup in 7 days.

There are a variety of antiplatelet therapies that could be tried, but aspirin is the most common and most tested. Starting on the patient on aspirin would be indicated at this point.

Since the patient has intermittent claudication, the prognosis is generally good. The patient has a good chance of improvement with medication and lifestyle changes.

All patients with Peripheral artery disease should have their LDL-cholesterol lowered to <100 mg/dL. Note that chronic kidney disease and diabetes can cause falsely elevated ABls. This is not present in this case, but itis
possible. This is due to calcinosis caused by glycosylation in diabetes.

We have also received emails stating that they feel that CT angiography should be accepted. However, CTA exposes the patient to radiation and iodinated contrast (can cause severe allergic reactions) and is more expensive.

Ultrasound is a better choice.

11.title: Abdominal Pain
11.chiefComplaint: Abdominal pain, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath
11.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute hepatitis, chronic hepatitis, Acute HIV infection, Acute drug-induced liver injury, community acquired pneumonia, aspiration pneumonia, chronic liver disease.
The patient has developed an acute hepatitis A infection from his cruise ship travels. His vomiting episodes resulted in the development of aspiration with a corresponding pneumonia, Another cause of acute liver injury is
acetaminophen toxicity, so an acetaminophen level would be useful. if the acetaminophen level were elevated, it would be imperative that N-acetyl-cysteine be initiated.

The patient's elevated liver enzymes and jaundice are likely caused by an infectious case, considering patient's lack of prior medical history and fever. As Hepatitis A is transferred through the fecal-oral route, contact
precautions should be initiated. Family members in close contact with the patient may consider getting immunized for Hepatitis A as a post-exposure prophylaxis. Hepatitis A is often prevalent in low socioeconomic areas
where there is a lack of adequate sanitation.

If the hepatitis panel were negative, further work-up would be considered, such as copper levels (Wilson's Disease), transferrin saturation and ferritin levels (hemochromatosis).
HAV infection usually results in an acute, self-limited illness and only rarely leads to fulminant hepatic failure. Fulminant hepatic failure occurs more commonly in patients with underlying liver disease, particularly chronic

hepatitis C virus infection.

Recent ATS/IDSA guidelines state that aspiration pneumonia should be treated like community acquired pneumonia and anerobic coverage should not be added unless the patient has a lung abscess or empyema.

The cruise ship travel and profoundly elevated transaminases are highly suspicious for acute viral hepatitis A (fecal-oral transmission). His episodes of vomiting led to aspiration pneumonia. Management is supportive: IV fluids, antiemetics, oxygen for hypoxia, and antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia per ATS/IDSA guidelines (treat as community-acquired pneumonia; no anaerobic coverage needed without abscess/empyema). Acetaminophen is contraindicated with hepatic injury. Admit to inpatient unit.

12.title: Burning During Urination
12.chiefComplaint: Dysuria, purulent urethral discharge, scrotal swelling
12.caseSummary:
Differential: Urethritis, Epididymitis, Gonorrhea, Syphilis, HIV, HSV.

Chlamydia is the most common bacterial STI. The organism is an intracellular pathogen. Patients who are contract chlamydia are often co-infected with gonorrhea (40% of women, 20% of men), so it is recommended to treat

for both pathogens empirically.

Cases of chlamydia are often asymptomatic, with 80% of women and 50% of men reporting no symptoms. In this case, the presence of purulent urethral discharge, dysuria, and scrotal swelling gives you clues that this patient
has contracted an infection.

It is important to screen for all STIs on this visit as the patient may have a co-infection of one or more of the STIs (Gonorrhea, HIV, Hep C, Hep B, syphilis, HSV). The Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), a DNA probe test on
first-catch urine, is first-line for the diagnosis of chlamydia, but a culture is also acceptable. Treatment should be empirically given, and the patient's partners should be treated as well.

Treatment for chlamydia is to give Azithromycin (oral one dose) or doxycycline (oral x 7 days).

13.title: Abdominal Pain
13.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, H. Pylori infection, B-cell lymphoma, gastric cancer, cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, viral gastroenteritis.

The HPI demonstrates patient's extensive use of ibuprofen for his chronic osteoarthritis. Suspicion is therefore high for patient developing NSAID-induced gastropathy. NSAIDs block both COX-1 and COX-2, impairing
production of gastric prostaglandins which maintains healthy mucosa. The condition should first be treated conservatively before other more invasive tests, such as an EGD (esophagogastroduodenoscopy), should be
considered. If the patient does not improve with conservative treatment in the next 2-4 weeks, an EGD would be indicated. An EGD was not pursued since the patient improved with the removal of NSAIDs and the
administration of a prescription of a proton-pump inhibitor. Antibiotics were not given as patient was negative for H. Pylori. Other risk factors could be targeted as nonpharmaceutical therapy, such as smoking and alcohol
use. In addition to Tylenol, topical pharmaceutical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel) are first-line for chronic osteoarthritis. The patient could try this as an alternative to oral NSAIDs for his knee pain.

To be more specific about the question about why points would be taken away for doing an endoscopy: This is excellent example of a case that is frequently seen on the USMLE. The case is there to see if you will restrain from
ordering invasive tests. The important piece of the case is in the history that the patient has been using excessive amounts of Ibuprofen. His symptoms have only been going on for a week. Conservative management is key to
have the patient stop NSAIDs and give a PPI/H2 and have the patient follow-up. If the patient continues to worsen, then you order invasive tests. The patient is medically stable. The patient does have risk factors (two being
his smoking status and his age), but there is no rush to do invasive tests.

15.title: Chest Pain
15.chiefComplaint: Pleuritic chest pain, relieved by leaning forward
15.caseSummary:
Differential: Myocardial infarction, Myocardial Ischemia, Peptic Ulcer Disease, Pulmonary embolism, Aortic Dissection, Aortic stenosis, Esophageal Rupture, Esophageal Spasm, Acute gastritis, GERD, Coronary artery
vasospasm, Angina Pectoris, Esophagitis, Cardiac tamponade.

As this patient does not have any previous medical history and did not suffer from a recent viral infection, he is likely suffering from idiopathic pericarditis. It follows a brief, benign course after treatment with anti-
inflammatory medication. First-line treatment includes a non-steroidal inflammatory drug (NSAID) and colchicine. The treatment could be accompanied by a proton-pump inhibitor to prevent the development of
gastrointestinal ulcers, which was proven to be effective in recent clinical trials.

Invasive treatment is not warranted in this patient as the echocardiogram only demonstrated a small effusion. Effusions that are symptomatic or are considered moderate to large effusions (>2 cm) may be treated with a
pericardiocentesis or other surgical procedure.

If the patient develops refractory pericarditis that is unresponsive to NSAIDs/colchicine, then glucocorticoids could be used. Typically, pericarditis that presents as such is usually caused by autoimmune pathologies.
Uremic pericarditis is another pathology that has an alternative treatment — the empiric treatment is dialysis.

Customers have asked why this patient does not have elevated WBC, ESR, or CRP. These would support the diagnosis of pericarditis, but they are neither sensitive nor specific for acute pericarditis. In the acute phase, these

markers may remain normal and only be present on follow-up.
15.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a man with no significant past medical history who presents with acute chest pain that is pleuritic (worse with inspiration) and positional (relieved by leaning forward). He has no history of recent viral infection, making this likely idiopathic pericarditis. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. Echocardiogram reveals a small pericardial effusion — no tamponade physiology. Troponin is negative, ruling out MI. First-line treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) PLUS colchicine — colchicine reduces symptoms and decreases rate of recurrent pericarditis. Add a PPI/H2 blocker for GI protection with high-dose NSAID therapy. Rest until symptoms resolve — activity can trigger recurrence. Pericardiocentesis is NOT indicated for small, asymptomatic effusions (only for moderate/large effusions > 2 cm or tamponade). Transesophageal echo is unnecessary — transthoracic echo is sufficient.

16.title: Cough
16.caseSummary:
Differential: Tuberculosis, atypical bacterial pneumonia (chlamydia pneumoniae, nocardia), nosocomial pneumonia, community-acquired pneumonia, tracheitis, bronchitis.

Pneumocystis Jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is the most common respiratory infection in HIV-infected patients. It is often seen in patients with a CD4 count of <200 who are not being treated by antiretroviral therapy or receiving
prophylactic antibiotic therapy. PCP Prophylaxis is initiated when patients fall below a CD4 count of 200, and Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is the first-line prophylactic antibiotic for patients that do not have a sulfa allergy.

Candida vulvovaginitis is the most common gynecological complaint of HIV-positive women. Topical antifungal therapy such as clotrimazole is first line therapy, but if patient is experiencing recurrence or a resistant strain,
imidazole or flucanozole may be used.

17.title: Weight Loss and Night Sweats
17.chiefComplaint: Painless cervical lymphadenopathy, weight loss, night sweats
17.caseSummary:
Differential: Hodgkin's lymphoma, Cat Scratch Disease (Bartonella Henslae), Breast Cancer, Metastases, Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, infectious mononucleosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), tuberculosis.

Hodgkin's lymphoma is a cancer derived from B-cells and is characteristically associated with the histological finding of Reed-Sternberg cells. Reed Sternberg cells are noted to have ‘owl-eyed’ nucleoli, surrounded by clear
cytoplasm. The cells are positive for CD15 and CD30. A lymph node biopsy will confirm the diagnosis. The patient will often present with painless cervical lymphadenopathy along with nonspecific constitutional symptoms.
Prognosis of a patient with Hodgkin's lymphoma can be determined after a PET or contrast-enhanced CT scan, which will show the dissemination of the disease. Staging is as follow for the disease:

- Stage |: Disease is limited to one single lymph node or one other site.

- Stage Il: Disease is within 2 or more lymph nodes on the same side of the diaphragm.

- Stage Ill: Disease is within lymph nodes on both sides of the diaphragm.

- Stage IV: Disease is outside of the lymph nodes.

Hodgkin Lymphoma is treated with chemotherapy and accompanied by radiation therapy in the early-stages of the disease. First-line chemotherapy treatment for Hodgkin Lymphoma is usually ABVD - Adriamycin,

Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine.
17.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and constitutional B-symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever). Hodgkin's lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy defined by Reed-Sternberg cells — 'owl-eyed' nucleoli with clear cytoplasm, CD15+ and CD30+. Excisional lymph node biopsy (NOT FNA) is required for diagnosis to preserve architecture for immunophenotyping and cytogenetics. CXR is initial screening. PET/CT for staging: Stage I (single node), II (≥2 nodes same side of diaphragm), III (both sides), IV (extranodal). Treatment: ABVD chemotherapy (Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine) ± radiation for early stage. Check albumin as prognostic indicator. Screen for HIV and EBV, which can mimic lymphoma.

17.intro: Painless cervical lymphadenopathy, weight loss, night sweats
17.history:
{{patient_name}} presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and constitutional B-symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever). Hodgkin's lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy defined by Reed-Sternberg cells — 'owl-eyed' nucleoli with clear cytoplasm, CD15+ and CD30+. 18.title: Constipation and Malaise
18.caseSummary:
Differential: Crohn's Disease, Diverticulosis, Ileus, Ischemic colitis, Ulcerative Colitis, Bowel obstruction secondary to surgical intervention

The patient has colorectal cancer. The most common form of colorectal cancer is adenocarcinoma of the colon, and is the third most common form of cancer. It stands as the third most common form of cancer mortality in
the United States, as well, in both men and women. Clinical symptoms of colorectal cancer can be classified based on their location - adenocarcinoma localized to the left colon present with symptoms of obstruction or
decreased stool caliber; while right colon masses present with signs of bleeding, such as iron deficiency anemia.

The patient would need to be followed up frequently at first and then every 3-6 months. The patient should get routine stool guaiac tests, annual CT/MRI scans of the abdomen/pelvis and chest x-rays for up to 5 years. A
repeat colonoscopy should initially be done at the one year, and then every three years following (assuming negative colonoscopy). CEA levels should be checked every 3-6 months (post-operative CEA of <2-3 is associated
with a good prognosis). High CEA levels suggest liver involvement or other metastasis. 90% of recurrences occur within 3 years of surgery, so follow-up is important.

19.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with the classic triad of diverticulitis: LLQ pain, low-grade fever, and leukocytosis. He has changes in bowel habits with nausea and vomiting. He meets SIRS criteria (fever >100.4°F, WBC >12,000). 20.title: Palpitations
20.caseSummary:
Differential: Third degree block secondary to: Infection (Lyme disease, viral myocarditis), increased vagal tone, progressive cardiac conduction disorders; Lenegre disease — fibrosis/sclerosis, Lev Disease (calcification),
cardiomyopathy, congenital AV block, hyperkalemia, hyper/hypothyroidism, iatrogenic effects.

Third Degree AV Block may be caused by an extensive list of pathologies, and results in a complete dissociation between supraventricular impulses to the ventricles. The most common cause of third-degree AV block is
coronary ischemia that involves the conduction system. It often presents with symptoms of syncope, dizziness, and hypotension. It is usually a bradycardic rhythm.

ECG will demonstrate P and QRS complexes that share no relationship. Patients can be temporarily stabilized with a transcutaneous pacer, but will require the placement of a permanent pacemaker.
Causes of Third-Degree AV Block:

- Pathologic: Myocardial ischemia, cardiomyopathy (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis), myocarditis (Lyme Disease, viral myocarditis), endocarditis with abscess, hyperkalemia, hypervagotonia

- _ latrogenic: AV nodal blocking medications (IE - Beta-blockers), post-cardiac surgery, post-catheter ablation

- Congenital AV Block

It is unlikely that this patient has a congenital disorder because 90% of patient with congenital heart block are symptomatic within 30 years. The patient's TSH was normal, so this is unlikely thyroid related. Chemistries were
normal and the CBC was normal, so this is unlikely due to an infectious etiology, but it would be reasonable to get a lyme titer. The patient has no history of any autoimmune diseases, and the ESR is normal, so this is
unlikely. The patient may have been on various anti-hypertensives in the past, but she is currently only taking hydrochlorothiazide. Troponin is negative so infarction is not likely.

The most likely cause is due to fibrous degeneration of the heart due to normal aging exacerbated by the patient's hypertension. It is not known about the patient's compliance with her anti-hypertensive medications. This

patient is symptomatic and has a complete heart block, so she should be put on a cardiac monitor, placed on a temporary pacer, and then taken to surgery and given a permanent pacemaker.

Third-degree AV block has an extensive differential: coronary ischemia (most common), fibrosis/sclerosis of conduction system (Lenegre/Lev disease — likely in this patient given age and HTN), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, hyperkalemia, thyroid disorders, iatrogenic (AV nodal blockers), and congenital (unlikely — 90% symptomatic by age 30). TSH normal, troponin negative, chemistries normal, ESR normal, CBC normal — infectious and inflammatory causes unlikely. Most likely: fibrous degeneration of conduction system from aging + hypertension. Management: temporary transcutaneous/transvenous pacemaker, then permanent pacemaker placement.

21.title: Abdominal Pain
21.chiefComplaint: Alternating diarrhea/constipation, abdominal pain relieved by defecation
21.caseSummary:
Differential: Irritable bowel syndrome, Colorectal Cancer, Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's Disease, Ulcerative Colitis), Infectious (parasites), Lactose intolerance, Celiac disease

Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is an idiopathic disorder that is defined by irregular activity of the gastrointestinal system. Symptoms include diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, and bloating. [BS is classically noted to be
relieved by defecation. There are certain alarm symptoms that require further work-up, and suggest a more serious pathology, such as iron-deficiency anemia with unexplained cause, active bleeding in the gastrointestinal
tract, weight loss, and early satiety.

Irritable bowel syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other etiologies should be ruled out first. The Rome IV Criteria defines IBS as a patient with recurrent abdominal pain and at least two of the following:
-Abdominal pain improves upon defecation

-Onset is associated with changes in stool frequency

-Onset is associated with change in stool appearance

It is possible that the patient has other diagnosis as mentioned above such as colon cancer, infectious (parasites), lactose intolerance, or celiac disease. It is unlikely that the patient at age 29 has colon cancer, although it is
possible. The patient has had no sick contacts and has had no history of travel, so an infectious source is unlikely. It is possible that the patient has lactose intolerance, so a trial of lactose free diet is warranted with patients
with IBS. Loperamide should be given as an as needed medicine for the diarrhea and with a caution not to overtake this as this could exacerbate the diarrhea. Since the patient's symptoms are in the mild category, and they
are not causing significant impairment, conservative management is warranted. This would include exclusion of gas-producing foods (beans, onions, celery, carrots, raisins, bananas, apricots, prunes, brussels sprouts, wheat
germ, pretzels, and bagels). High fiber diet and exercise are also improtant. Smooth muscle relaxants such as Dicyclomine or hyoscyamine may treat the patient in the short term, but long term efficacy has not been
demonstrated.

In this case, conservative measures such as diet change and exercise should be tried first before starting on any medications other than loperamide for the diarrhea. If the patient comes back for a followup visit and continues
to have symptoms other medications other than previously mention can be trialed. TCAs (amitriptyline, imipramine, nortriptyline, and desipramine) and SSRis (fluoxetine, sertraline) are treatments for IBS which can be
attempted.

The main point in this case is to treat conservatively and avoid any invasive testing such as colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy. The worrisome differential diagnosis can be neatly eliminated based on general lab workup, stool

sample, and fecal occult blood tests.
21.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a 29-year-old who presents with alternating diarrhea and constipation, abdominal pain relieved by defecation, and bloating — meeting Rome IV criteria for IBS (recurrent abdominal pain + ≥2 of: improvement with defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool appearance). ESR and CRP are normal, ruling out inflammatory bowel disease. Stool studies are negative for infectious etiology. IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out celiac disease (anti-tTG, anti-endomysial antibodies), C. difficile, parasites, and colorectal cancer. Conservative management is key: high-fiber diet, lactose-free trial, exercise, trigger food avoidance. Loperamide PRN for diarrhea, antispasmodics (dicyclomine/hyoscyamine) PRN. Colonoscopy/sigmoidoscopy is NOT appropriate — invasive testing loses points in stable patients with normal screening labs. TCA/SSRI for refractory cases at follow-up.

22.title: Found Unconscious
22.chiefComplaint: Found unconscious, respiratory depression, suspected overdose
22.caseSummary:
Differential: Hypoglycemia, Hyperglycemia, Toxic ingestion, Opioid overdose, Hypothyroidism

Tricyclic antidepressants poisoning often presents with sedation and may include symptoms of delirium or hallucinations. Cardiac arrhythmias is one of the major side effects to look out for. A common mnemonic for TCA

poisoning is the ‘three C's’: Coma, convulsions, and cardiac.

Cardiovascular effects mainly present with widened QRS, prolonged QT, or prolonged PR intervals. It is important to initiate cardiac monitoring and to provide sodium bicarbonate when the patient is presenting with these
EKG changes. Sodium bicarbonate works in two ways: The increase in serum pH favors the non-ionized form of the TCA, so less of the drug binds to sodium channels. The increase in extracellular sodium overcomes the
blockade of sodium channels carried about by TCAs. Lidocaine is another alternative. For those that are hemodynamically unstable, they may require a shock.

TCAs have also been associated with anticholinergic properties, precipitating seizures. Diazepam or phenobarbital are often used to prevent actively seizing patients

Hypotension is also another common presentation in TCA overdose — IV fluids, sodium bicarbonate, and epinephrine/norepinephrine if needed are given to maintain patient's blood pressure status. This is caused by TCA’s
ability to block alpha-1 receptors. Blocking alpha-1 receptors causes sinus tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, vasodilatation, hypotension and asystole. This also exerts a number of effects on the central nervous system, leading

to drowsiness coma, respiratory depression and seizures.

The patient is hypoxic with a pulse ox of 75% (ABG also shows that the patient is hypoxic) Oxygen should be started, IV access gained, and patient should be intubated and put on a ventilator. The patient should have a head
CT when stable to rule out any acute injury that could be exacerbating the overdose.

Aspirin and Acetaminophen levels are standard for overdose in case the patient were to take these in conjunction with the TCA which in common in many overdose cases.

Activated charcoal is the most beneficial if the patient took the TCA within 2 hours which is unknown in this patient. It should still be given. Once the patient is awake and can protect her airway after 24 hours, the patient can
be extubated. Psychiatry should be consulted in this case to determine disposition. The patient may require an inpatient stay in the psychiatric inpatient unit. The patient's blood pressure was >70mmHg. If it were lower,
epinephrine would have to be administered or another agent to increase her blood pressure. The patient's EKG resolves with time and with alkalinization.

23.title: Shortness of Breath
23.chiefComplaint: Progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, LE edema
23.caseSummary:
Differential: Congestive heart failure, Acute renal failure, Acute myocardial infarction, Acute respiratory distress syndrome, Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, Pneumonia, Pulmonary embolism, Pulmonary edema

This patient is experiencing congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, often referred to as systolic dysfunction heart failure. His heart failure is likely the result of old age and his prior myocardial infarction that
damaged his cardiac tissue. This creates a condition where the heart is unable to contract and pump enough blood to meet his cardiac needs. The most common cause of this form of heart failure is cardiac ischemia and
coronary artery disease. The condition presents with symptoms of fluid overload, such as pulmonary congestion, shortness of breath, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (difficulty breathing), orthopnea (difficulty breathing in
recumbent position; relieved by elevation of the head will pillows), and nocturia. When heart failure becomes severe, the patient could also experience hemoptysis, resulting from increased pressure in the alveolar capillaries.
Macrophages in the alveoli will digest the red blood cells, creating hemosiderin-laden macrophages, also known as heart failure cells.

Diagnosis of congestive heart failure is done through the patient's clinical history and physical exam, and is supported by a number of diagnostic tests. On auscultation, an 3 murmur will be heard on exam, and pulmonary
‘edema will present with rales and crackles and may also be accompanied by expiratory wheezing. Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is elevated in these patients, and an echocardiogram will demonstrate reduced ejection
fraction in systolic dysfunction.

The easiest way to think about this is defined by the New York Heart Association (NYHA) Classification of congestive heart failure.

NYHA class |: Symptoms only occur with vigorous activities, such as playing a sport. Patients are nearly asymptomatic;
NYHA class II: Symptoms occur with prolonged or moderate exertion, such as climbing a flight of stairs or carrying heavy packages. Slight limitation of activities;
NYHA class Ill: Symptoms occur with usual activities of daily living, such as walking across the room or getting dressed. Markedly limiting;

NYHA class IV: Symptoms occur at rest;

This classification helps with treatment. In general, this is how you would treat a patient with CHF:

Mild CHF (NYHA Class | to II):

Restrict sodium intake (<4 g sodium) and mildly restrict physical activity;

Start loop diuretic if patient is volume overloaded or pulmonary congestion is present

Use an ACE inhibitor as first-line agent;

Mild to moderate CHF (NYHA Class I! to Ill):

Start a diuretic (loop diuretic) and an ACE inhibitor,

Add a beta-blocker;

Moderate to Severe CHF (NYHA class Ill to IV):

Add digoxin to loop diuretic and ACE inhibitor and beta blocker;

Add spironolactone

The patient has moderate to Severe CHF, so the patient should be started on a loop diuretic to diurese excess fluids, continue his ACE inhibitor (patient already on lisinopril), and give a beta blockers. Carvedilol is the beta-

blocker of choice. In the COMET trial, carvedilol led to significant improvement in survival compared with metoprolol.

The patient might be able to be managed as an outpatient, but since this is the first time that the patient has had symptoms, the patient would benefit from inpatient admission so that the workup could be complete more
quickly (echocardiogram to assess ejection fraction) as an inpatient. The patient would receive IV diuretics which work more quickly. Once the patient is feeling better, the patient can be discharged and switched to PO

diuretics and be followed up as an outpatient.

Lifestyle changes also prevent the development of heart failure: reducing obesity, smoking cessation, reducing alcohol consumption, decreasing sodium intake, controlling chronic conditions of hypertension, lipid disorders,
and diabetes.

25.title: Generalized Pain
25.diagnosis: Sickle Cell Anemia with Acute Chest Syndrome and Pneumonia
25.chiefComplaint: Generalized pain, fever, respiratory distress, fatigue
25.caseSummary:
Differential: Sickle cell anemia, Sickle cell trait, Upper respiratory tract infection, Pneumonia, Acute chest syndrome

This patient has been diagnosed with sickle cell disease, which has precipitated the development of acute chest syndrome along with a lobar pneumonia. It is important to hospitalize the patient, start IV fluids, give IV pain
medication (morphine or dilaudid), and start the patient on hydroxyurea which increases the fetal hemoglobin which prevents the RBC from sickling as much. The patient likely had a sickle crisis due to an infection, which
sickle cell patients are prone. Giving a cephalosporin is the treatment of choice, so giving IV ceftriaxone is the treatment here for the infection. Before antibiotics are given, a blood culture should be obtained.

Sickle cell disease is a genetic disease (autosomal recessive) causes by a single amino acid substitution on the beta globin chain (a valine is substituted) which results in the hemoglobin S.
Sickle cell anemia does not present clinically before 6 months of age because of the protective effect from the uninvolved Hemoglobin F. But after 6 months of age, the usual clinical manifestations include infection (usually
respiratory), failure to thrive, unexplained fever, and irritability. Before routine newborn screening for sickle cell disease, young children often presented with dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome), which is a swelling of the dorsum

of the hands or feet, associated with pallor and fever.

These children are especially prone to bacterial infections such as pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae B and Salmonella. Historically, infections have been the primary cause of death during early childhood, Since fevers
alone can increase sickling, any febrile child with sickle cell anemia should be given IV hydration to prevent further sickling, and empiric antibiotic therapy should be given. One reason for the high rate of infections in children
with sickle cell disease is that they are functionally asplenic. Because the spleen acts as a sponge for these abnormal sickled cells, subclinical intermittent episodes of intrasplenic vaso-occlusion occur causing local splenic
infarcts. Therefore, by the age of 8 years, sickle cell patients are completely functionally asplenic (due to infarction). All sickle cell patients are given prophylactic penicillin, especially during childhood,

It has been shown that patients with sickle cell anemia become clinically asymptomatic if the amount of Hemoglobin S in the circulating blood is less than 30%. One way to accomplish this is to transfuse children with normal
red blood cells, thereby diluting down their amount of Hemoglobin S, and also shutting off their own hematopoiesis to a large degree. Thus, children with significant morbidity can be placed on a transfusion protocol, in
which patients are transfused about every 2 to 4 weeks, indefinitely. The goal of transfusion therapy is to lower the percentage of hemoglobin S to <30% at all times, and to keep the hematocrit below 46%, reducing blood

viscosity.

Bone marrow transplantation - This has been performed successfully to treat sickle cell anemia, but it is not routinely performed due to matched donor availability and risk of complications. However, it may be more cost-
effective in the long run,

With the current obstetric practices, sickle cell disease can be diagnosed as early as within the first weeks of pregnancy through methods such as chorionic villous sampling, but it is also diagnosed through the newborn
screening tests. The symptoms associated with sickle cell anemia during an acute crisis stems from vaso-occlusion. Common symptoms include dactylitis, auto-splenectomy, pulmonary vaso-occlusive crisis (chest pain and
shortness of breath), renal papillary necrosis (hematuria and proteinuria).

The patient does not seem to be getting routine care from a hematologist, and therefore a consult is required so that the patient may be placed on medications for his condition. Sickle cell anemia patients are often placed
on hydroxyurea, a widely used medication for sickle cell disease, which is capable of stimulating fetal hemoglobin production. Penicillin is also given for prophylaxis due to autosplenectomy - making patients susceptible to
encapsulated organisms.

26.title: Shortness of Breath
26.chiefComplaint: Chronic cough, dyspnea, recurrent infections, poor growth
26.caseSummary:
Differential: Cystic fibrosis, Failure to thrive, Asthma, Malabsorption syndrome, Sinusitis, Bronchiectasis

Cystic Fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition due to a mutation in a chloride channel (gene CFTR, located on chromosome 7). It is most common in the Caucasian population. The majority of these cases are detected
through newborn screening in the United States, but individuals that were not born through standardized healthcare systems often remain undiagnosed. A positive newborn screening is indicated by an elevated sweat
chloride level of greater than 60 mEq/L. Abnormal sweat chloride testing is sufficient to diagnose cystic fibrosis in infants as well as non-infants.

The CFTR channel regulates chloride movement in a number of epithelial cells, including the respiratory tract, the pancreas, sweat/salivary glands, intestines, and the reproductive system. This results in thick secretions that
are difficult to clear, and are therefore more prone to developing infections. The most common infectious pathogens include H. influenzae, Staph. Aureus, Pseudomonas Aeruginosa, and Bulkholderia cepacia. Common
findings in patients with cystic fibrosis on physical exam include wheezing, increased anterior/posterior diameter of the chest, digital clubbing, and failure to thrive/difficulty in gaining weight. There are a number of
complications that are associated with cystic fibrosis, but respiratory complication is the number one contributor to morbidity/mortality. Chest physiotherapy and additional antibiotics may improve the condition, but a lung
transplant may be necessary in candidates with severe disease.

The treatment in this case is to stabilize the patient which is done by giving supplemental oxygen and IV fluids. Next, the patient is given enzyme replacement therapy, vitamins, lV antibiotics, and chest physical therapy.

The defect in chloride transport leads to thick, viscous secretions affecting the lungs, pancreas, GI tract, and reproductive system. Diagnosis is made by elevated sweat chloride test (>60 mEq/L). CXR shows hyperinflation and bronchiectasis. Management includes pancreatic enzyme replacement, fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, airway clearance techniques, and aggressive treatment of pulmonary infections.

28.title: Pelvic Pain
28.chiefComplaint: Bilateral pelvic pain, fever, purulent discharge
28.caseSummary:
Differential: Pelvic inflammatory disease, Acute appendicitis, Dysmenorrhea, Endometriosis, Urinary tract infection, Ectopic pregnancy
This patient has pelvic inflammatory disease. She meets clinical criteria with adnexal tenderness, abdominal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis. The patient's cervical culture is positive for N.
gonorrhoeae. A CBC, gram stain, and culture will solidify the diagnosis.

Pelvic inflammatory disease is consequence of untreated sexually-transmitted infections and results in complications such as ectopic pregnancy, Fitz-Hugh Curtis syndrome, and infertility. The pathology results from an
ascending infection from the vagina that travels up the cervix and into the uterus, entering the intraperitoneal cavity through the fallopian tubes.

Gonorrhea and chlamydia are the principal organisms that cause pelvic inflammatory disease, but most cases are thought to be polymicrobial in nature. Risk factors for PID include multiple partners, recent history of
douching, prior history of PID, and cigarette smoking. Clinical symptoms are lower abdominal pain specifically localized to the uterine and adnexal regions, tenderness in the bimanual exam, cervical motion tenderness

(chandelier sign), vaginal bleeding/discharge, nausea/diarrhea, and painful urination.

Outpatient oral treatment of mild to moderate PID are ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, with or without metronidazole. Severe PID is treated with IV cefotetan or cefoxitin, accompanied by oral doxycycline.
Normal labs and vaginal ultrasound rule out other causes of abdominal pain. The patient should be admitted to the hospital (patient is nulliparous and has a fever with abdominal pain) and be given IV antibiotics. Other
criteria for inpatient treatment include elevated WBC, adolescence, peritoneal symptoms, uncertain diagnosis, failure to respond to 48 hours of outpatient management, inability to tolerate outpatient treatment, pregnancy
and immunodeficiency.

‘Once the patient is feeling better, you can stop the IV fluids and IV antibiotics. Then you can switch the patient to PO doxycycline which should continue for 14 days. When the antibiotics are complete, the patient can

followup with you at your office in 14 days. Itis also important to treat her sexual partner as well and to educate on safe sex practices.
28.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a sexually active young woman presenting with bilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, fever, and leukocytosis. Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection from the lower genital tract — commonly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, though polymicrobial. Diagnosis is clinical based on CDC criteria: uterine/adnexal tenderness + cervical motion tenderness (minimum). Complications: tubo-ovarian abscess, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain. Treatment: empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics covering chlamydia, gonorrhea, and anaerobes — ceftriaxone 250mg IM once + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 14 days + metronidazole 500mg PO BID x 14 days. Partner treatment essential. Screen for other STIs. Admit if severe, TOA, pregnant, or failed outpatient treatment.

28.intro: Bilateral pelvic pain, fever, purulent discharge
28.history:
{{patient_name}} is a sexually active young woman presenting with bilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, fever, and leukocytosis. Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection from the lower genital tract — commonly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, though polymicrobial. Diagnosis is clinical based on CDC criteria: uterine/adnexal tenderness + cervical motion tenderness (minimum). Complications: tubo-ovarian abscess, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain. Treatment: empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics covering chlamydia, gonorrhea, and anaerobes — ceftriaxone 250mg IM once + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 14 days + metronidazole 500mg PO BID x 14 days. Partner treatment essential. Screen for other STIs. Admit if severe, TOA, pregnant, or failed outpatient treatment.

PID diagnosed clinically. Cervical motion tenderness + adnexal tenderness + fever + discharge. Ceftriaxone IM + doxycycline x14d + metronidazole x14d. Rule out ectopic. Partner treatment.

29.title: Vaginal Bleeding
29.caseSummary:
Differential: Spontaneous abortion, Polyps, Adenomyosis, Fibroids, Bleeding disorders, Gynecological cancers, Urinary tract infection, Polycystic ovarian syndrome, Primary ovarian insufficiency.

The patient presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, which is defined as bleeding outside the normal pattern of a woman's menstrual cycle. Often, the cause of menstrual abnormalities are hormonal imbalances - this
includes disorders such as hyperprolactinemia (pituitary dysregulation, prolactinoma), thyroid dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian syndrome. Bleeding disorders may present with abnormal uterine bleeding, so this may be
ruled out with coagulation studies.

Itis also important to evaluate other causes/locations of bleeding, |.E. the rectum, the vagina, urethra, and cervix. A pelvic ultrasound can determine whether structural pathologies are the cause of bleeding — such as polyps,

fibroids, and cancerous growths.

When all other causes of abnormal uterine bleeding causes are ruled out, it can be assumed that anovulation is the cause. Anovulation is the most common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding in women of childbearing age.
The ovaries produce estrogen but do not undergo ovulation, Therefore, no corpus luteum and progesterone is not released . Continual estrogen stimulation of the endometrium results in increased growth of the blood

supply and sloughing at irregular times,

Hormone therapy (IUDs, oral contraceptives, etc) are given to regulate the patient's menstrual cycle. In this case, the patient can just get high dose oral estrogens. Only estrogen therapy would be the fastest to stop the
bleeding. This should be no more than 21-25 days. Combined progestin/estrogen therapy can be used as well, but this may take longer to stop the bleeding.

This therapy should be avoided in women with absolute contraindications to estrogen therapy (women with DVT, history of MI, history of cerebrovascular accident, history of malignancy, or inherited thrombophilia such as
Factor V leiden or prothrombin gene mutation). Women with the following risk factors can be safely treated with estrogen for short periods (less than 4 weeks): Hypertension, Diabetes, SLE, smoking.

In this case, the patient has a thickened endometrial lining. High dose progestins could also be used as this will inhibit further endometrial growth and organize and support the estrogen-primed endometrium which will
allow effective sloughing upon hormone withdrawal. If the patient does not have a thickened endometrium, progestins are unlikely to be effective.

In summary, estrogen only therapy is faster. Combined estrogen/progestin can be used, but it may take longer. Progestin only is only effective if a patient has anovulatory bleeding with a thickened endometrium.
If you get a patient who has contraindications to estrogen therapy, then you can use progestins or surgery. You can also use tranexamic acid but progestins and surgery would be preferred.

We have received questions about why an endometrial biopsy is considered invasive. The patient is 33 years old and has no risk factors for malignancy (age > 50, taking Tamoxifen, PCOS, obesity, diabetes). The patient does

not require a biopsy. The cause of the thickened endometrial lining is due to estrogen stimulation without progesterone being released due to anovulation.

Diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out pregnancy, structural lesions (fibroids, polyps), thyroid dysfunction, coagulopathy, and malignancy. Workup: HCG (rule out pregnancy/complications), CBC (assess anemia from blood loss), TSH/prolactin, pelvic ultrasound (rule out structural causes), endometrial biopsy if age >45 or risk factors. Treatment depends on severity and fertility goals: hormonal regulation with combined OCPs or cyclic progestins. If acute heavy bleeding: high-dose estrogen or IV conjugated estrogens. Iron supplementation for anemia.

30.title: Pain in Right Arm
30.diagnosis: Colles' Fracture of Right Arm / Domestic Abuse
30.chiefComplaint: Right wrist pain, swelling, and deformity after fall
30.caseSummary:
Differential: Domestic abuse, neurological abnormalities causing balance issues, substance abuse, Accident Prone.
A Colles’ fracture is defined a distal radial fracture that is usually dorsally displaced. The most common mechanism of injury is when a patient falls on his/her outstretched hand when in dorsiflexion. Physical exam will present

with tenderness on palpation of the distal forearm on the lateral side. In the case of this patient, if the fracture remains stable, closed reduction of the dorsally displaced radius fracture followed by casting/splinting is essential

for the patient's fracture to heal properly. Pain medications should also be administered.
Complications of a Colles’ fracture include neurovascular complications (IE - median nerve injury, vascular ischemia, compartment syndrome), as well as malunion, co-occurring scaphoid fractures, and ligamentous injuries.

An important take-away from this case is how to handle a patient with domestic abuse. Physicians should reassure the patient that they are available for support. The patient should be connected with social work so that they
may be offered options for counseling and safe havens. It is important to continually offer ongoing support and concern when patients come into the physician's office in order to foster an open line of communication, as the

patient may be reluctant at first to disclose their situation.

Although the patient denies that she is being abused (which is common due to fear of retaliation by the abuser), there is enough evidence to suspect this. The patient has bruises on cheeks, forehead, fractured right ribs
which all are not likely a result from a fall down some stairs. After doing a skeletal survey, the patient is noted to have old fractures of her left ribs. Thus, the patient is either accident prone or more likely is being abused at
home. Substance abuse is also on the differential and a simple urine toxicology screen can rule this out (although the patient may have been sober for many days prior to coming to the doctor which would result in a
negative urine toxicology screen). No tract marks were seen or other evidences that would infer that the patient had problems with substance abuse.

‘Once the diagnosis is made, you can splint the patient's arm, order ibuprofen and PRN oxycodone and counsel the patient regarding domestic abuse. It is also important to counsel the patient regarding a safety plan and

refer the patient to a support group and a social worker.

31.diagnosis: Duodenal Ulcer with Iron Deficiency Anemia
31.caseSummary:
Differential: Goesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer, gastroenteritis, gastric ulcer, nonulcer dyspepsia, biliary colic or cholecystitis, pancreatitis, irritable bowel syndrome.

Peptic ulcer disease occurs when the mucosal wall of the duodenum and stomach are disrupted, resulting in recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, often located in the epigastric region. A number of factors can contribute to
the development of peptic ulcer disease, such as: H. Pylori Infection; Drugs (NSAIDs, SSRI); Alcohol; Smoking; Physiologic stress (IE burns, head trauma, surgery); Acid hypersecretion.

The most common cause of peptic ulcer disease is H. Pylori infection. It disrupts the mucosal lining by increasing acid secretion and inhibiting bicarbonate production. In the case of this patient, he has developed a duodenal.
ulcer secondary to H. Pylori infection. Pain derived from duodenal ulcers are classically improved with food ingestion. Upper endoscopy is the gold standard for evaluating patients with peptic ulcer disease, especially through
mucosal biopsy. Other diagnostic methods include urease breath test, fecal H. Pylori antigen testing, and H. Pylori serum antibody testing. A major complication of peptic ulcer disease is bleeding, which could lead to

hemorrhage and perforation. Triple therapy consists of clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and a proton-pump inhibitor. Quadruple therapy is given to those that may have resistance to clarithromycin — which includes metronidazole,

bismuth, tetracycline, and a proton-pump inhibitor.

32.title: Abdominal Pain
32.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute cholecystitis, Acute appendicitis, Gastritis, Acute pancreatitis, Acute hepatitis, Acute cholangitis, Gastritis, Right sided pneumonia, Small bowel obstruction, Renal colic.

This patient is experiencing acute calculous cholecystitis, which typically presents with constant, prolonged right upper quadrant pain that radiates to the right shoulder. Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and
anorexia. The classic situation is fatty food ingestion occurs prior to onset of pain. The patient meets the “Four F's rule” which is fat, forty, fertile, and female which increases her risk of developing acute cholecystitis. Regarding
the need for antibiotics, the guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) recommend that antimicrobial therapy be instituted if infection is suspected on the basis of laboratory (more than 12,500 white cells
per cubic millimeter) or clinical findings (temperature of more than 385 ), and radiographic findings (eg, air in the gallbladder or gallbladder wall). Routine antibiotics are also recommended in older patients or those with
diabetes or immunodeficiency. The patient in this case has a fever of 38.6, so antibiotics are necessary. There are a number of approaches and you can use one of the following:

Ampicillin-sulbactam, Piperacillin-tazobactam, Ticarcillin-clavulanate, Combination third generation cephalosporin (optional metronidazole) (i. ceftriaxone with optional metronidazole), fluoroquinolones with optional

metronidazole (i. ciprofloxacin with optional metronidazole), or monotherapy with a carbapenem (i.e. meropenem).

If the patient is a good surgical candidate such as this patient, then the patient should have a cholecystectomy during their initial hospitalization as this decreases hospital readmission rates and mortality. Surgery should be
consulted and the patient should be scheduled for a cholecystectomy. The case will end at this point.

Question of Sepsis/infection:
The patient has a fever of 38.6, but she is unaware of how long it has been going on. The patient is hemodynamically stable and has no other vital sign abnormalities. The question is whether the patient has Systemic
Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS). Clinically, SIRS is the occurrence of at least 2 of the following criteria:

= «36°C (96.8 °F) or >38 °C (100.4 °F)

- Heart Rate > 90/min

-  Tachypnea > 20 breaths/minute

-  Leukocytosis > 12 x 1049/L or 10% bands

The patient meets only 1 of the SIRS criteria, so a pan-culture including a chest X-ray, a urine culture, and a blood culture is not necessary in this case. However, points would not be taken off for doing these things. All clinical

signs point to acute cholecystitis.

Acute cholangitis is a strong second differential as the patient has symptoms that suggest a presentation of acute cholangitis as well: RUQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis. However, on ultrasound, there would likely be evidence
of cholestasis as well as biliary dilatation,

Note about imaging: Although a CT scan will confirm the diagnosis, this is not the first recommended radiological exam for the diagnosis of Acute cholecystitis. Abdominal ultrasound is the recommended first radiological
exam for diagnostic confirmation. If ultrasound is negative or unclear, then a HIDA scan should be done. However, in this case, the ultrasound is positive an no further radiological exams are needed.

Murphy's sign is a diagnostic measure that suggests acute cholecystitis. When the right upper quadrant region is deeply palpated, inspiratory arrest occurs. Other diagnostic findings include: Leukocytosis with left shift
(bandemia); Abdominal ultrasound: gallbladder edema, wall thickening, and subserosal edema may be seen.

If the abdominal ultrasound is unclear, then a HIDA/cholescintigraphy scan is performed. Failure to visualize the gallbladder after 4 hours post-injection of the dye is diagnostic of acute cholecystitis.

Initial management of patients with acute cholecystitis include NPO status, supportive care (Intravenous fluids, pain control), and empiric intravenous antibiotics. The patient is admitted to the hospital and laparoscopic
cholecystectomy is usually performed within 48 hours.

Another subset of cholecystitis is emphysematous cholecystitis, and these patients are generally more toxic appearing. Gas will be seen within the gallbladder wall, and right upper quadrant abdominal wall crepitus is seen on

physical exam. Older men with diabetes are often affected by emphysematous cholecystitis

33.title: Altered Mental Status
33.chiefComplaint: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, cognitive decline
33.caseSummary:
Differential: Neurodegenerative dementia, Progressive supranuclear palsy, Parkinson disease dementia, Dementia with lewy bodies, Multiple system atrophy, Cerebrovascular disease, Alzheimer disease.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus is caused by excess cerebrospinal fluid that collects within the cerebral ventricles and spinal cord, resulting in increased pressure on the brain. A number of pathologies can result in normal
pressure hydrocephalus, which includes subarachnoid hemorthage, chronic meningitis, and other pathologies that prevent cerebrospinal fluid resorption. The mnemonic for normal pressure hydrocephalus is recalled by
remembering the 3 W's: wacky (altered mental status), wobbly (gait abnormalities), and wet (incontinence).

Patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus will demonstrate widened ventricles. Other findings, such as white matter lesions and cerebral aqueduct atrophy may also be present. A MRI is more sensitive in detecting normal
pressure hydrocephalus. A CT may also present with these findings, but it will not be as sensitive for this pathology. For diagnostic purposes, the patient can undergo a LP and drain 30 to 50 ml of CSF and then test the
patient's gait and cognitive function before, and 30-60 minutes after the procedure. The treatment for NPH involves placing a ventriculoperitoneal shunt.
33.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient presenting with the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus: (1) gait disturbance ('magnetic gait' — feet feel stuck to floor), (2) urinary incontinence, and (3) progressive cognitive decline/dementia. NPH is one of the few reversible causes of dementia and must be recognized early. CT/MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, without obstruction. LP opening pressure is NORMAL (<18 cm H2O) — this distinguishes NPH from obstructive hydrocephalus. High-volume LP (30-50 mL CSF removal) with pre- and post- gait assessment is diagnostic: improvement in gait after CSF removal supports the diagnosis and predicts response to VP shunting. Definitive treatment: ventriculoperitoneal shunt.

34.chiefComplaint: Severe headache, blurry vision, severely elevated BP
34.caseSummary:
Differential: Malignant hypertension, Acute intracranial hemorrhage, Cluster headaches, Cushing's syndrome, Illicit drug use, Intracranial neoplasm, Partial seizure.
This patient is experiencing hypertensive emergency, as he is experiencing elevated blood pressure: Systolic blood pressure > 180 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure >120 mm Hg AND evidence of end-organ damage.
In the case of this patient, he is showing signs of hypertensive retinopathy and acute renal failure with elevated creatinine.

Here are a number of manifestations that may present in an individual with hypertensive emergency: Acute myocardial infarction; Hypertensive encephalopathy; Intracranial hemorrhage; Dissecting aneurysm; Acute renal

failure; Flash pulmonary edema.

Hypertensive crises are often brought on by an exacerbation of underlying hypertension, frequently caused by noncompliance of anti-hypertensive therapy. Other causes include: medication side effects, recreational drug use,
pregnancy, anatomic abnormalities (atherosclerosis, renal artery stenosis), and endocrinopathies.

Patient care includes immediate admission to the hospital, IV administration of a titratable anti-hypertensive agent, and continuous monitoring of blood pressure, neurological status, and urine output.
A general treatment for the following presentations include

- Hypertensive encephalopathy: Labetalol

- Pregnancy: Labetalol

- Aortic Dissection: Labetalol + Esmolol

35.title: Seizure
35.caseSummary:
Differential: Infection (meningitis), trauma (intracranial hemorrhage), metabolic derangements, drug abuse, hepatic failure, gastrointestinal bleeding, Alcohol withdrawal.
Alcohol withdrawal has a wide range of symptoms, that can range from tremulousness to delirium tremens. This patient is presenting with delirium tremens, which is characterized by autonomic instability, hallucinations,

agitation, and altered mental status. Patients that present with seizures or delirium tremens are advised to receive IV therapy with benzodiazepines. It should also be noted that benzodiazepines are metabolized by the liver,
and those with severe liver disease should avoid long-acting benzodiazepines. Lorazepam and oxazepam should be used in this case due to their shorter half-life, preventing the unwanted side effect of over-sedation.

For patients that do not have liver disease, long-acting benzodiazepines would be preferred as they provide a lower chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. This includes chlordiazepoxide and diazepam. Refractory
delirium tremens is common in patients with chronic alcohol abuse, as they have developed low endogenous GABA concentrations or resistant GABA receptors.

Haldol/antipsychotic administration is controversial in delirium. It is commonly used, but academically, antipsychotics are considered poor practice to be used in delirium tremens as this can lower the seizure threshold. The
patient does have visual hallucinations of seeing snakes under the bed. It is reasonable to use haldol to treat, but it is also reasonable to not treat, so this is an optional order. He should be rehydrated with normal saline as
well as given thiamine, 86, and folate. The patient can then be maintained on Naltrexone. The patient's liver function is elevated but not elevated enough that would contraindicate naltrexone (naltrexone can also cause liver
‘enzymes to peak, so monitoring of the liver enzymes is warranted). The lability of these patients requires close monitoring, and therefore an intensive care unit transfer is necessary for this patient.
35.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with new-onset seizure, altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), tremors, and visual/tactile hallucinations (formication). History reveals chronic heavy alcohol use with abrupt cessation 24-72 hours prior. This is alcohol withdrawal progressing to delirium tremens — a medical emergency with 5-15% mortality if untreated. Pathophysiology: chronic alcohol enhances GABA inhibition and suppresses NMDA glutamate excitation. Abrupt withdrawal → loss of GABA tone + rebound glutamate hyperactivity → CNS hyperexcitability. The CIWA-Ar score quantifies severity and guides treatment. Management: benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) — symptom-triggered or fixed-schedule dosing until sedated but arousable. Thiamine before glucose (prevent Wernicke's). IV fluids for dehydration. Correct electrolytes (hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia common). Admit to ICU for severe DTs. Rule out other causes of seizure: CT head, EEG, tox screen, metabolic panel.

36.title: Headache
36.chiefComplaint: Severe headache, fever, stiff neck, photophobia, rash
36.caseSummary:
Differential: Meningitis, Intracranial abscess, Epidural abscess, Migraine, Subarachnoid hemorrhage, Sinusitis, Encephalitis

The patient in this case has bacterial meningitis. The patient has the classical findings of bacterial meningitis which include nuchal rigidity, photophobia, and a positive Kernig’s sign and Brudzinsk's sign. The lumbar puncture
shows a gram positive S. pneumoniae. The order is important. It is important to get a blood culture, start empiric antibiotics, get a CT scan, then get a LP. Note that giving antibiotics should not change the lumbar puncture
result as long as the LP is within 4 hours of giving the first dose of the antibiotic. The patient should be given Ceftriaxone and vancomycin since this is a normal adult. This patient should also be given Dexamethasone which
needs to be given before or with the first antibiotic treatment.

Close contacts do not need to be treated in this case because the bacterial is S. pneumoniae. If the patient had N. meningitidis, then close contacts would need to be treated with Rifampi, Cipro, or Ceftriaxone.
We have received emails about why dexamethasone is the only accepted steroid treatment. Most of the studies that study bacterial meningitis neurologic complications use dexamethasone. Using a different medication that

has not been studied as well would be a mistake.
36.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe headache, fever, photophobia, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status. Exam reveals positive Kernig's sign (pain with knee extension when hip flexed 90°) and Brudzinski's sign (involuntary hip/knee flexion with passive neck flexion). Petechial/purpuric rash is present — meningococcemia causes DIC and purpura fulminans. This is a medical emergency. Do NOT delay antibiotics for CT or LP. Blood cultures + LP with CSF analysis (opening pressure, cell count with differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture). CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose (<40 or <2/3 serum), elevated protein, Gram-negative diplococci. Empiric antibiotics: ceftriaxone 2g IV + vancomycin + dexamethasone (before or with first dose). Add ampicillin if Listeria risk (age >50, immunocompromised). Droplet precautions for meningococcal. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone).

38.title: Yellowing of Eyes
38.chiefComplaint: Painless jaundice, weight loss, dark urine, clay-colored stools
38.caseSummary:
Differential: Cholangiocarcioma, Metastatic cancer to the liver, Pancreatic cancer, Gilbert disease, autoimmune hepatitis, Primary biliary cirrhosis, Hepatitis, acute/chronic hepatocellular injury, choledocholithiasis,
cholangiocarcinoma.

This patient presenting with an ill-defined mass at the head of the pancreas, and is likely suffering from pancreatic adenocarcinoma. 90% of pancreatic cancers are adenocarcinomas, and the majority are localized to the head
of pancreas. It is a highly lethal malignancy, and the 4th leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States. The cancer is often linked to males and cigarette smoking. Symptoms include painless, extra-hepatic
obstructive jaundice, weight loss, and post-prandial epigastric pain.

Surgical resection is the only curative treatment — despite this, prognosis is poor despite complete resection. The Whipple procedure is utilized for resection of pancreatic head tumors, which includes removal of the head of
the pancreas, as well as a portion of the duodenum, the gallbladder, and some of the stomach. Once a biopsy is obtained and the patient's diagnosis is set, then itis important to consult the oncologist and the surgeons for
recommendations for treatment. Once the diagnosis is made, the case will end.
38.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, clay-colored stools, pruritus, and weight loss — classic for malignant biliary obstruction. Courvoisier's sign: palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient = malignancy until proven otherwise (most commonly pancreatic head adenocarcinoma). Pancreatic cancer most commonly arises in the head of the pancreas (70%), causing early obstructive jaundice. Late presentation is the rule — most are unresectable at diagnosis. Workup: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (pancreatic protocol — dual-phase) for staging. CA 19-9 tumor marker (not diagnostic but prognostic and monitors recurrence). ERCP/MRCP for biliary drainage if needed. Biopsy via EUS-FNA. If resectable (localized, no vascular involvement, no mets): pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure). If unresectable: palliative biliary stenting, chemotherapy (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel or FOLFIRINOX). Poor prognosis — 5-year survival <10%.
