122.title: Painful Rash
122.chiefComplaint: Fever, widespread painful rash, mucosal involvement
122.caseSummary:
Differential: Erythema multiforme, Generalized bullous fixed drug reaction, Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, Linear IgA bullous dermatosis

The patient in this case has Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) from his exposure to Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole. Drug exposure is the most common cause of SJS. The next most common in children is a bacterial infection
with Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Because of this, it is recommended that tests for Mycoplasma pneumoniae to screen for this.

It is important to get bacterial and fungal cultures of the wounds because it is common that patients with SIS will have bacterial infection and sepsis.

The treatment for SJS is mainly supportive. The first thing to do would be to stop the offending agent which in this case would be the Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole. The patient should then be admitted to the ICU and be

given IV fluids and pain medication.

As this patient is presenting in the initial stages of SJS, Cyclosporine should be given as it has been shown to help slow progress of SIS in early stages.
122.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset fever, widespread painful target-like lesions, bullae, epidermal detachment (<10% BSA = SJS, 10-30% = SJS/TEN overlap, >30% = TEN), and mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital). Nikolsky sign positive (epidermis sloughs with gentle pressure). Most commonly triggered by medications: sulfa antibiotics, anti-epileptics (lamotrigine, phenytoin, carbamazepine), allopurinol, NSAIDs, within 1-8 weeks of exposure. This is a medical emergency. Immediately discontinue offending drug. Admit to burn ICU. Supportive care: fluid/electrolyte management, wound care, infection prevention, nutritional support, ophthalmology consult. Systemic steroids controversial — not universally recommended. IVIG or cyclosporine may be considered. SCORTEN score for prognosis.

123.title: Leg Pain
123.caseSummary:
Differential: Muscle strain, Cellulitis, venous insufficiency, lymphedema, popliteal cyst.

The patient has classic symptoms of a Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT). The patient has risk factors for a DVT which include: smoking, obesity, tenderness at area of interest, pitting edema, calf swelling 3cm larger than the
other leg, and dilation of superficial veins. The patient would have a High Probability of DVT on the Wells Score.

The D-Dimer results will be elevated. This would be optional since the patient has a high probability due to risk factors of having a DVT. A calf ultrasound (doppler) should be done to confirm the diagnosis. The patient should
then be put on anticoagulants. The options for anticoagulation are: LMW herparin (Lovenox) + Warfarin (Coumadin) OR Lovenox + dabigatran OR Lovenox + edoxaban OR Rivaroxaban monotherapy OR Apixaban
Monotherapy. The patient should be counseled on smoking cessation and put on a weight loss diet.
123.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and erythema. Risk factors: Virchow's triad — stasis (immobilization, long travel), hypercoagulability (malignancy, OCPs, pregnancy, thrombophilia), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma). Exam: Homan's sign unreliable. Measure leg circumference difference. Wells criteria determines pretest probability. If low probability → D-dimer. If D-dimer elevated or high probability → compression ultrasound (proximal DVT). Treatment: most DVT → anticoagulation with DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) or LMWH bridge to warfarin. Duration: provoked = 3 months, unprovoked = 6-12 months or indefinite. NO routine thrombectomy or IVC filter unless anticoagulation contraindicated. Compression stockings for symptom relief and post-thrombotic syndrome prevention.

124.title: Chest Pain
124.chiefComplaint: Acute chest pain — evaluate for STEMI
124.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute Aortic Dissection, Pulmonary embolism, Pericardial tamponade, Esophageal rupture
The patient has an ST-elevated inferior myocardial infarction (STEMI). ST elevations will be present in leads II, 
III, and aVF. The patient should immediately be started on dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): Aspirin plus a 
P2Y12 inhibitor (Ticagrelor is preferred; Clopidogrel is also accepted). A beta blocker and atorvastatin should 
also be initiated. Cardiology should be consulted and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) — angioplasty 
with stent placement — should be performed, as this is the preferred reperfusion strategy.
In the USMLE, immediate PCI is available, so fibrinolytic therapy is not required. If fibrinolysis is ordered, 
partial credit will be awarded, but full credit requires PCI as the preferred approach.
Regarding antiplatelet therapy: Ticagrelor and Prasugrel are the preferred P2Y12 agents, but Prasugrel is not 
yet available as an order in the USMLE database. Clopidogrel is acceptable and will receive full credit, as the 
distinction between P2Y12 agents is considered out of scope for the exam. Note that these agents are 
antiplatelet drugs, not anticoagulants — anticoagulation with heparin is a separate consideration in STEMI 
management.
Once appropriate treatment has been initiated, the patient will improve and the case will end.

125.title: Chest Pain
125.chiefComplaint: Chest pain, hypotension, clear lungs, elevated JVP
125.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute Aortic Dissection, Pulmonary embolism, Pericardial tamponade, Esophageal rupture

This case is similar to case 124, but the medical treatment is very different. Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction (RVMI) is typically caused by occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA). The presence of hypotension,
elevated jugular venous pressure, and tricuspid regurgitation murmur is suggestive of a RVMI. RVMI tends to be associated more frequently with vagal symptoms, such as bradycardia, nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, and

pallor.

Just like in case 124, the treatment is reperfusion. Cardiology should be consulted and an angioplasty with a stent placement should be performed (now known as percutaneous coronary intervention). This is the preferred
treatment. In the USMLE, you will have access to immediate treatment, so you do not need to do medical fibrinolysis treatment. If you do fibrinolysis treatment, you will gain points, but you will not get full credit as the
preferred method is angioplasty with a stent placement. The patient should be given ticagrelor or prasugrel (Prasugrel is not yet an order on the USMLE) as anticoagulants. Ticagrelor and prasugrel are preferred to
Clopidogrel, but Clopidogrel will still be accepted as this knowledge is out of scope for the test.

Aspirin and anticoagulants should be given, but beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, morphine, and nitroglycerin should be avoided in RVMI. Beta blockers can negatively affect the heart rate and contractility. Nitrate and

opioids can negatively affect preload and worsen the problem.

EKG will show that the patient has ST elevation in leads V4. Once treatment has taken place, the patient will feel better, and the case will end.
125.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chest pain, hypotension, clear lung fields, elevated JVP, and Kussmaul's sign. ECG shows ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) with ST elevation in V1 > V3 and ST elevation in V4R (right-sided leads) — indicating RV involvement. RV infarction occurs in ~30% of inferior MIs (usually RCA occlusion). RV is preload-dependent — nitroglycerin and morphine can cause dangerous hypotension because they reduce preload. Treatment: AVOID nitrates and diuretics (reduce preload → worsen RV output). Give IV fluids aggressively to maintain RV preload. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation. REPERFUSION: emergent PCI (preferred) or fibrinolysis. If hypotensive despite fluids: dobutamine (inotrope). Atropine for bradycardia. Admit to CCU.

126.title: Shortness of Breath
126.chiefComplaint: Shortness of breath and fatigue with dizziness
126.caseSummary:
Differential: ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction, Acute Aortic Dissection, Pulmonary embolism, Pericardial tamponade, Esophageal rupture

This case is similar to case 124 and 125 but the presentation is different. The patient does not present with chest pain. She presents with atypical symptoms of shortness of breath and fatigue with some dizziness. This atypical
presentation is more common in elderly women and with patients who have diabetes and hypertension. The patient has ST depression in leads |, II, V4, VS, V6. This suggests a subendocardial ischemia.

Just like in case 124/125, the treatment is reperfusion. Cardiology should be consulted and an angioplasty with a stent placement should be performed (now known as percutaneous coronary intervention). This is the
preferred treatment. In the USMLE, you will have access to immediate treatment. Patients with Unstable angina or NSTEMI do not benefit from fibrinolysis. The patient should be given ticagrelor or prasugrel (Prasugrel is not
yet an order on the USMLE) as anticoagulants. Ticagrelor and prasugrel are preferred to Clopidogrel, but Clopidogrel will still be accepted as this knowledge is out of scope for the test.

Aspirin and anticoagulants should be given. Beta-blockers should be given. Morphine and nitroglycerin are not necessary as the patient does not complain of pain. Anticoagulants should also be given (UFH, Bivalirudin,
‘enoxaparin, or fondaparinux). Once treatment has taken place, the patient will feel better, and the case will end,

127.title: Rash
127.chiefComplaint: Petechiae, purpura, easy bruising in well child
127.caseSummary:
Differential: Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, Liver Disease, Hereditary thrombocytopenia, Myelodysplastic Disorders
This patient in this case has Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). The patient most likely developed ITP after having a recent viral infection. ITP patients will have platelet counts less than 100,000/microL with a normal white

blood cell count and hemoglobin. The majority of children develop ITP after a recent viral illness. The patient has gingival bleeding and petechiae. This would classify the patient as a grade III/IV between moderate and severe.
The patient will require treatment with either glucocorticoids, IVIG, or IV anti-D.

The patient is at risk for potentially severe bleeding if injured, so the patient should be counseled to avoid contact sports as well as to avoid antiplatelet medications like Aspirin and NSAIDs. Depending on the treatment

choice, the patient can be treated either inpatient or outpatient. Once the patient gets treatment, he will improve.
127.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with sudden onset petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and possibly mucosal bleeding in an otherwise well-appearing child. No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no fever, no bone pain — distinguishes from leukemia. ITP is an autoimmune destruction of platelets (antibodies against GPIIb/IIIa). Often preceded by viral URI or vaccination 1-4 weeks prior. Labs: ISOLATED thrombocytopenia (platelets <100K, often <20K). Normal Hb, normal WBC, normal peripheral smear (except low platelets). Bone marrow biopsy NOT needed in typical childhood ITP. Treatment: most children (>80%) recover spontaneously within 6 months. If platelets >20K and no bleeding → observation only. If <10K or significant bleeding → prednisone 2-4 mg/kg/day or IVIG or anti-D (if Rh+). Avoid IM injections, contact sports, NSAIDs/aspirin.

128.title: Depression
128.caseSummary:
Differential: Physiologic hypercortisolism, Adrenal Tumor, Metastatic Disease, Exogenous Cortisol use.

The patient in this case has Cushing Disease. The symptoms the patient is suffering include: weight gain, plethora face (moon face), hirsutism (facial hair growth), thinning hair, and depression. Dexamethasone test is the standard test to test for Cushings syndrome. 24-hour urinary cortisol can also be used. The new test which is not currently on the USMLE is the late-night salivary cortisol test.

Once Cushings Syndrome has been established, the cause of it should be determined. This is best by measuring the ACTH. If the ACTH is high (above 20 pg/mL), then the cushings syndrome is ACTH-dependent. This could be caused by a pituitary tumor, ectopic ACTH, or corticotropin-releasing hormone secretion. The patient should have a brain MRI done to look for a pituitary tumor.

If the ACTH is low (below 5 pg/mL), then this would be an ACTH-independent disease. If this were the case, a CT of the adrenal glands should be done to look for an adrenal mass.

In this case, the ACTH is high. An MRI of the brain should also be done to look for a pituitary tumor. In this case, a pituitary tumor is found. Neurosurgery should be consulted to remove the tumor. No points would be given for treatment for depression like SSRIs or a consult to mental health. The treatment is not mental health services; it is fixing the underlying condition causing her depression.
128.hpiNarrative:
{{patient_name}} presents with depression, fatigue, weight gain, moon facies, hirsutism, thinning hair, and amenorrhea for six months. This is Cushing disease from a pituitary adenoma — not primary major depressive disorder.

Workup: pregnancy test (amenorrhea); dexamethasone suppression test or 24-hour urine cortisol to confirm hypercortisolism; ACTH level — high ACTH (>20 pg/mL) indicates ACTH-dependent Cushing (pituitary vs ectopic); brain MRI for pituitary tumor when ACTH is elevated.

Definitive treatment is transsphenoidal resection (neurosurgery consult). SSRIs or psychiatry consult alone do not treat the underlying endocrine cause.

129.title: Facial Pain
129.chiefComplaint: Sudden severe electric shock-like facial pain
129.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute herpes zoster, Painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy, Idiopathic painful trigeminal 
neuropathy, postherpetic trigeminal neuropathy.
The patient has classic Trigeminal neuralgia. The most common cause of trigeminal neuralgia is compression 
of the trigeminal nerve root (80-90% of cases). The compression is typically caused by a vascular loop. 
The criteria to diagnose trigeminal neuralgia include: having recurrent episodes of facial pain in one area of 
the trigeminal nerve; pain lasting seconds to 2 minutes; severe intensity; sharp/electric pain which can be 
precipitated by innocuous stimuli within the affected trigeminal distribution. 
MRI/CT scan should be done to rule out lesions such as tumor or neurovascular compression. The first line 
treatment for trigeminal neuralgia is Carbamazepine or Oxcarbazepine. Gabapentin can also be used, but this 
is second line. Surgery does not need to be consulted as medical treatment should occur and fail prior to 
involving surgery. The patient may improve over time and may not require surgical intervention. In this case, 
the patient will improve on Carbamazepine or Oxcarbazepine, and the case will end.

129.hpiNarrative:
{{patient_name}} presents with classic trigeminal neuralgia — recurrent episodes of severe, sharp, electric shock-like facial pain in one area of the trigeminal nerve distribution, lasting seconds to two minutes, often precipitated by innocuous stimuli (light touch, chewing, wind). The most common cause is compression of the trigeminal nerve root (80–90% of cases), typically by a vascular loop.

Differential: acute herpes zoster, painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy, idiopathic painful trigeminal neuropathy, postherpetic trigeminal neuropathy.

Workup: neurologic exam including cranial nerves; CBC to exclude infection; BMP/CMP; MRI or CT head to exclude tumor or neurovascular compression.

First-line treatment is carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine; gabapentin/pregabalin are second line. Surgery is not indicated until medical therapy fails.

130.title: Cough
130.chiefComplaint: High fever, cough, GI symptoms, hyponatremia
130.caseSummary:
Differential: Typical pneumonia, Lung cancer, Lung abscess, Bronchitis, Pulmonary embolus, Legionella pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, and Bronchiectasis.

This patient has Legionella pneumonia (also known as Legionnaires disease which is in the Atypical pneumonia category). This is a real scenario with an outbreak of Legionella due to a contaminated air conditioning system at
a convention, The clue is in the history where his other colleagues are also sick. Legionella pneumonia should be high on the differential as outbreaks can occur through contaminated water sources. Patients with Legionella

pneumonia also tend to present with Gl symptoms of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

After doing a physical exam (which reveals lung findings consistent with a consolidation), basic labs should be obtained, including sputum culture and gram stain, as well as a chest X-ray. The patient is young without
comorbidities, so this case can be handled as an outpatient. The fastest way to get a positive test would be to test for the Legionella urine antigen. Although it can be falsely negative, if the Legionella urine antigen is positive,
then this would confirm the diagnosis. Legionella urine antigens can be detected as early as one day after symptom onset and can be detected from days to weeks. A typical culture can also be done, but the ideal testing
would be the Legionella urine antigen.

‘Once the diagnosis is made, the patient should be treated with antibiotics. The first line treatment is Levofloxacin or Azithromycin. Alternative antibiotics include: Moxifloxacin, Clarithromycin, Erythromycin, Ciprofloxacin,

Doxycycline. Once the patient has been treated with antibiotics, he will begin to feel better, and the case will end.

133.chiefComplaint: Chronic low back pain, morning stiffness improved by exercise
133.caseSummary:
Differential: Chronic Nonspecific Back Pain, Fibromyalgia, Vertebral Compression Fracture, Sacroiliac joint infection, Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis

The patient has Ankylosing Spondylitis. The patient has classic symptoms of Ankylosing Spondylitis which include back pain, morning stiffness which improves with activity, Dactylitis, Heel pain, and a history of Psoriasis.
Psoriasis increases the likelihood of Ankylosing Spondylitis.

Initial evaluation should be a physical exam focusing on extremities and eyes (to look for uveitis). Once a physical exam is completed, Rheumatoid Factor, CRP/ERP, HLA-B27, and an X-ray of the pelvis should be obtained.
‘Once the diagnosis of Ankylosing Spondylitis is made, treatment should be with a TNF-inhibitors (Etanercept, Infliximab, Adalimumab, Golimumab (Not an order on the USMLE), or Certolizumab pegol (Not an order on the
USMLE)). Both Interleukin 17 inhibitors are not yet available as orders on the USMLE which include Secukinumab and Ixekizumab. Interleukin 17 inhibitors are also treatment options for Ankylosing Spondylitis, but as noted

above, these are not yet orders on the USMLE. NSAIDs are typically first line treatment, but as stated in the history, the patient has been using a lot of NSAIDs and continues to have symptoms.

Once the correct treatment is given, the patient will begin to feel better after a week, and the case will end.
133.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic low back pain (>3 months), morning stiffness (>30 min) that IMPROVES with exercise and WORSENS with rest. Inflammatory back pain pattern (vs mechanical — worsens with activity). Associated: sacroiliitis, limited spinal mobility (Schober test), enthesitis, peripheral arthritis, uveitis. Young male predominance. Strong association with HLA-B27. Diagnosis: X-ray/MRI of SI joints — sacroiliitis (bamboo spine in advanced disease). Elevated ESR/CRP. Treatment: NSAIDs first-line (excellent response — diagnostic feature). Physical therapy — maintain posture and mobility. If NSAIDs insufficient → TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept). IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab) also effective. Do NOT recommend bed rest — makes it worse. Exercise program essential.

134.title: Scrotal Pain
134.chiefComplaint: Unilateral scrotal pain, swelling, gradual onset
134.caseSummary:
Differential: Testicular Torsion, Trauma, Inguinal hernia, Testicular cancer, Referred pain.

The patient has Acute Epididymitis. Due to the age of the patient and his risk sexual practices, his acute Acute Epididymitis is most likely from an infectious source. Imaging is not required in this case as the physical exam
shows tenderness and swelling of the epididymis. The patient has a positive cremasteric reflex (this usually would be negative in testicular torsion).

The most common infectious causes of Acute Epididymitis are N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. These should be tested for, but they are commonly negative in those who do not have lower urinary tract symptoms such as

in this case. As the patient practices anal sex, coliform bacteria in the rectum could be the cause of his Acute Epididymitis.
This case can be treated as an outpatient. The patient can be treated with oral antibiotics, NSAIDS, application of ice to the scrotum, and scrotal elevation,
The antibiotic choice in this case would be ceftriaxone plus a fluoroquinolone to cover all the possible culprits of gonorrhea, chlamydia, and rectal flora.

After 48 hours of treatment, the patient will begin to feel better, and the case will end. The patient should be counseled on safe sex practices.

Caused by ascending infection: sexually active young men → Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Older men or post-instrumentation → E. coli, enteric organisms. 135.title: Muscle Weakness
135.diagnosis: Hyperkalemic Emergency secondary to ACE Inhibitor + NSAID
135.caseSummary:
Differential: Guillain-Barre syndrome, Hyperkalemic Periodic Paralysis, Pseudohypoaldosteronism

The patient has Hyperkalemia due to ACE Inhibitor Use and NSAID use. Hyperkalemia can manifest with symptoms which range from asymptomatic to having: nausea, vomiting, areflexia, weakness, flaccid paralysis,
paresthesias, and intestinal colic. ECG changes can include: tall, peaked T waves, wide QRS, PR prolongations, and a loss of P waves. This can progress to sine waves, ventricular fibrillation, and cardiac arrest.

ACE inhibitors will block angiotensin I! which will reduce aldosterone secretion which will reduce potassium secretion which will then raise the potassium serum concentration.
NSAIDs can lower renal renin secretion and impair angiotensin II-induced aldosterone release. This will decrease aldosterone which will reduce urinary potassium excretion which will then raise the potassium serum
concentration.

In this case, the patient had both an NSAID (indomethacin) and an ACE Inhibitor (lisinopril) which led to his hyperkalemia. The ACE Inhibitor should be stopped, and the patient should be given IV Calcium Chloride to prevent
cardiac arrhythmias. IV insulin + glucose (or albuterol nebulizer) should be given to temporarily shift potassium into the cells, and Kayexalate or Furosemide can be used to increase secretion of potassium.

Dialysis is an option, but in this case, less invasive treatment should be attempted first, and if the patient continues to be refractory from initial treatment, then dialysis can be considered,
The patient should be admitted to the inpatient unit as he will need cardiac monitoring and IV medications and fluids. Once treatment is given for 3-12 hours, the potassium will decrease, and the patient will feel better, and
the case will end.
135.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves, loss of P waves, widened QRS. Labs reveal severe hyperkalemia (K+ >6.5). Medication history: on ACE inhibitor for HTN and recently started NSAIDs for joint pain. ACEI reduces aldosterone → decreased renal K+ excretion. NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow → further decrease K+ excretion. Combined → dangerous hyperkalemia. Management: IMMEDIATE cardiac membrane stabilization — IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride (does NOT lower K+, PROTECTS the heart). Then shift K+ intracellularly: IV regular insulin + glucose, beta-agonist (albuterol nebulized), sodium bicarbonate if acidotic. Then eliminate K+: furosemide (if renal function adequate), sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate), patiromer, or hemodialysis if refractory. Discontinue ACEI and NSAIDs.

136.title: Shortness of Breath
136.chiefComplaint: Progressive dyspnea, dry cough, bilateral hilar adenopathy
136.caseSummary:
Differential: Tuberculosis, Preumoconiosis, Fungal Infection, lymphoma, Pulmonary fibrosis, HIV

The patient has Sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis can present in many different ways and can be diagnostically challenging in real life scenarios as it can affect many different organs in many different ways. However, in the USMLE, it

will be much more straight forward. Typical presentations can include: cough, malaise, cough, weight loss, dyspnea, and arthritis (typically involving the ankle and knees).

The presentation in this case of nonproductive cough, malaise, weight loss is also similar in HIV and Tuberculosis, so HIV and Tuberculosis tests should be done to rule these out. Chest X-ray will show bilateral hilar
lymphadenopathy and pulmonary function tests will show a restrictive pattern with reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity which is associated with a reduction in the DLCO.

First line treatment is glucocorticoids, typically prednisone. Alternative treatments include: Methotrexate, Azathioprine, and Leflunomide. There are other immunosuppressants that is outside the scope of the USMLE that are
alternatives.

After a month of treatment, the patient will feel better. A repeat chest X-ray can be done to verify that radiologically that the patient is improving,
136.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR. May have erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on shins), uveitis, parotid enlargement, lupus pernio (purplish facial plaques). Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology — more common in African Americans. Non-caseating granulomas are the pathologic hallmark. CXR staging: I (BHL only), II (BHL + parenchymal infiltrates), III (parenchymal only), IV (fibrosis). Labs: elevated ACE level (supports but not diagnostic), hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria (increased 1,25-vitamin D from activated macrophages in granulomas). Diagnosis: biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas + exclusion of other causes (TB, fungal, berylliosis). PFTs: restrictive pattern. Treatment: many resolve spontaneously (stage I). If symptomatic or progressive → corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day). Methotrexate or azathioprine for steroid-sparing. Anti-TNF for refractory. Monitor for TB reactivation before immunosuppression.

136.intro: Progressive dyspnea, dry cough, bilateral hilar adenopathy
136.history: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR. May have erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on shins), uveitis, parotid enlargement, lupus pernio (purplish facial plaques). Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology — more common in African Americans. Non-caseating granulomas are the pathologic hallmark. CXR staging: I (BHL only), II (BHL + parenchymal infiltrates), III (parenchymal only), IV (fibrosis). Labs: elevated ACE level (supports but not diagnostic), hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria (increased 1,25-vitamin D from activated macrophages in granulomas). Diagnosis: biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas + exclusion of other causes (TB, fungal, berylliosis). PFTs: restrictive pattern. Treatment: many resolve spontaneously (stage I). If symptomatic or progressive → corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day). Methotrexate or azathioprine for steroid-sparing. Anti-TNF for refractory. Monitor for TB reactivation before immunosuppression.

137.title: Wrist and Ankle Pain
137.caseSummary:
Differential: Infectious arthritis, Gout, Osteoarthritis, Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Psoriatic arthritis.

The patient has Rheumatoid arthritis. This should be suspected as the patient has inflammatory polyarthritis. Lab tests that can point to rheumatoid arthritis are a positive Rheumatoid factor (RF) and a positive anti-

citrullinated peptide antibodies. An ANA should be done to rule out lupus and other autoimmune diseases.
With the combination of radiological evidence, positive RF, elevated ESR/CRP, and negative synovial studies (for crystals and bacteria), then a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis can be confidently made.

‘Treatment is a combination of a NSAID and a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD). The preferred line of treatment for a DMARD would be methotrexate. Other alternative DMARDs include: hydroxychloroquine,
sulfasalazine, leflunomide, Etanercept, Infliximab, and Adalimumab.

Opioids should be avoided due to addiction concerns and because DMARDs are more effective in treating rheumatoid arthritis. After several weeks, the patient will begin to feel better, and the case will end.
137.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with symmetric polyarthritis involving small joints of hands (MCP, PIP), wrists, and ankles. Morning stiffness >1 hour. Joints are warm, swollen, tender. RA is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis. Key features: symmetric, polyarticular, involves hands/feet, spares DIP joints (distinguishes from osteoarthritis which involves DIP/PIP, Heberden/Bouchard nodes). Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, vasculitis, Felty's syndrome. Labs: RF (rheumatoid factor — 80% sensitive), anti-CCP (anti-citrullinated peptide — very specific >95%), elevated ESR/CRP. X-ray: periarticular osteopenia, joint space narrowing, marginal erosions. Treatment: early aggressive DMARDs — methotrexate first-line. Plus short-term prednisone bridge. If MTX inadequate → add biologic (TNF inhibitor — etanercept, adalimumab). Refer to rheumatology. Physical and occupational therapy.

138.title: Fatigue
138.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute Kidney Disease, Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), Medullary Cystic Kidney Disease, IgA Nephropathy, Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis, Fabry disease

The patient has end stage renal failure likely from diabetes mellitus and hypertension. This patient is not subtle with a creatinine of 9.24. The patient has primary metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap with full
respiratory compensation. The patient has too many metabolic abnormalities to be treated as an outpatient (including a potassium of 6), so the patient will require inpatient hospitalization and dialysis.

Nephrology should be consulted to help with the management of the patient. A kidney transplant will be needed as a long-term solution
Indications for dialysis include declining nutritional status, fatigue, malaise, mild cognitive impairment, hyperkalemia, refractory acidosis. The patient in this case easily meets these criteria,

‘Once the patient is put on dialysis, the patient will begin to feel better, and the case will end.

We have received emails regarding why this patient requires hemodialysis. The patient is symptomatic and has a creatinine of 9.24. The calculated eGFR based on a 60 year old would be 6 mL/min/1.73m2. The patient is
having memory problems, fluid overload, and a very low eGFR, the patient will require dialysis. Dialysis indications are the following: - eGFR < 10 mL/min/1.73m2, uremic encephalopathy (the patient has been having episodes

of confusion which is likely due to uremic encephalopathy), cognitive impairment, hyperkalemia, fatigue and malaise, persistent volume overload, and declining nutritional status. The patient clearly meets this criteria. Efforts
to treat the hyperkalemia with various medications prior to hemodialysis are not needed as hemodialysis will treat the hyperkalemia and other metabolic problems.

138.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive fatigue, weakness, anorexia, nausea, pruritus, edema, and oliguria. Labs: markedly elevated BUN/Cr, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia (low EPO), hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism. ESRD is irreversible loss of renal function (GFR <15). Most common causes: diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis. Management: renal replacement therapy — hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplant. Urgent indications for dialysis: AEIOU — Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalemia), Intoxication (toxins), Overload (volume), Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy). Treat anemia (EPO), manage mineral bone disease (phosphate binders, vitamin D, calcimimetics). Refer for AV fistula creation. Nephrology referral.

139.title: Lip Lesion
139.diagnosis: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lip
139.chiefComplaint: Non-healing ulcerated lesion on lower lip
139.caseSummary:
The patient has squamous cell carcinoma of the lip. This is a fairly straight forward case. You diagnose by a biopsy and then remove the tumor by consulting dermatology to perform Mohs surgery. Mohs surgery tends to be

the gold standard for removing facial tumors as it minimizes tissue loss.

The Mohs surgeon will remove a layer of area where the tumor was located and take the tissue, dye it, and look at the histology of the removed tissue. If there are still cancer cells in the specimen, the Mohs surgeon will go

back and remove more of the lesion until there is no more cancer. The patient will wait in the office while the Mohs surgeon looks at the tissue, so that the surgeon can remove more tissue if necessary. Mohs surgery will

preserve the most tissue and have the best cosmetic outcome which is important to most patients.

Mohs surgery is an outpatient procedure and can be done with local anesthetic. Once the surgery is completed, the case will end.
139.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with a non-healing, ulcerated, crusted lesion on the lower lip (sun-exposed area). Risk factors: chronic sun exposure, fair skin, smoking, immunosuppression. Actinic cheilitis is a premalignant condition — persistent scaling, crusting of lower lip. Progression to SCC: firm, ulcerated, bleeding lesion. Diagnosis: biopsy (shave or punch) — shows keratin pearls, atypical squamous cells. Treatment: surgical excision with clear margins (Mohs micrographic surgery for cosmetically sensitive areas). Prevention: sun protection, lip balm with SPF, smoking cessation. Monitor for regional lymph node involvement.

140.title: Headache
140.chiefComplaint: Chronic headache, transient visual loss, pulsatile tinnitus
140.caseSummary:
Differential: Intracranial tumor, Obstructive hydrocephalus, Choroid Plexus Papilloma, Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

The patient has Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension which is commonly known as Pseudotumor Cerebri. The cause of the elevated intracranial pressure is not known (which is why it is labeled idiopathic). However, obesity is a

risk factor as well as being female. The patient is obese and should attempt to lose weight which would improve her overall health.

ACT/MRI should be done to rule out an intracranial tumor or other gross abnormality. A lumbar puncture will show an increase opening pressure. CSF studies will be normal. The diagnosis can then be made of Pseudotumor
Cerebri.

The treatment for Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension is Acetazolamide which is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor which can reduce the rate of CSF production. Other medications can be tried if the patient is unable to tolerate

Acetazolamide such as Topiramate or Methazolamide.

‘Once the patient begins treatment, after a few days, she will begin to feel better, and the case will end.
140.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic daily headache (worse in morning, with Valsalva), transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, and diplopia (CN VI palsy from increased ICP). Fundoscopy: bilateral papilledema. IIH is elevated ICP without mass lesion or hydrocephalus, typically in obese women of childbearing age. Risk factors: obesity, recent weight gain, vitamin A excess, tetracyclines, OCPs, steroids. Diagnosis: MRI/MRV brain (normal — rules out mass, venous sinus thrombosis). LP: elevated opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) with normal CSF composition. Treatment: weight loss (most important), acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — reduces CSF production). Serial ophthalmology: visual fields, optic nerve exam. If vision threatened: optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting (VP or LP shunt). Discontinue causative medications.

142.title: Seizures
142.chiefComplaint: Neonatal seizures, maple syrup odor, poor feeding
142.caseSummary:
Differential: Beta-ketothiolase deficiency. Glycine encephalopathy, Methylmalonic acidemia, Propionic acidemia.

The patient has the signs of classic Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) which include: irritability, poor feeding, bicycling movements, focal dystonia, and seizures. The are 5 types of MSUD (Classic, Intermediate, Intermittent,
Thiamine-responsive, and E3-deficient). Classic MSUD is the most common. The amino acid levels are given to you because these orders are not present on the USMLE at this time. There are no orders for serum or urine
levels of glutamic acid, valine, isoleucine, or leucine. However, you must put together that high amino acid levels with the presentation to come up with the MSUD diagnosis.

The treatment for MSUD is a no-protein/low-protein diet. This specialized diet would be life-long much like PKU. The patient would not be able to breast-feed and would need a non-branched-chain amino acids (meaning
low, leucine, valine, isoleucine) formula. There is no specific diet order on the USMLE for a non-branched-chain amino acid diet, so a low-protein/no protein diet will suffice. It is recommended that all patients with MSUD be
treated with a thiamine to see if the patient has the Thiamine-responsive type. If there is no improvement after 4 weeks, then the thiamine treatment can be discontinued.

A potential long-term treatment of MSUD is liver transplantation. As the patient is only a week old, this discussion would happen at a later time and would depend on the outcome of diet modification.

Note that in this case, the CBC/CMP will be normal which is not abnormal as the patient seems to be suffering more neurological damage than metabolic issues. However, metabolic decompensation is a possibility, so the
patient should be followed closely. Admitting to the hospital/ICU is appropriate until the patient can be stabilized and amino acid levels returned to normal levels. MSUD is more severe than PKU as this can lead to death

The patient will have protein and ketones in the urine with an elevated serum ammonia and CRP.

143.title: Poor Feeding
143.chiefComplaint: Neonatal poor feeding, jaundice, vomiting on milk feeds
143.caseSummary:
Differential: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, Biliary atresia

The patient has the signs of classic galactosemia which include: jaundice, vomiting, hepatomegaly, poor feeding, lethargy, and cataracts. Other findings commonly seen that is not present in this case are: sepsis, diarrhea, and
acute liver failure. The cause of classic galactosemia is a deficiency of the galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT) enzyme.

With classic galactosemia, infants are typically born without complications and appear healthy. Most infants have neonatal screenings done, but these can take 7-30 days to return, After 1-2 days, the patient will begin to
show symptoms after serum galactose levels increase.

This is a difficult case as this may appear to be a routine breast-feeding neonatal jaundice case. It is tempting to just put the baby under bili-lights and advance the clock. However, there are concerning findings which include
elevated liver enzymes and bilateral cataracts (which would be missed if a HEENT exam is not done). These findings which would differentiate from a breast-feeding neonatal jaundice case.

The gold standard to detect classic galactosemia is to send for DNA sequencing (Sanger sequencing). This is not an order on the USMLE at this time, so clinical information and laboratory data should be used to guide your
diagnosis and treatment.

The treatment is to simply put the patient on a lactose and galactose free diet. The patient will need to stop drinking breast milk and switch to a soy-based infant formula. The patient will need to be admitted to the inpatient

unit and monitored. The patient will improve after the removal of lactose/galactose from the diet.

144.title: Short Stature
144.diagnosis: Turner syndrome with coarctation of the aorta
144.chiefComplaint: Short stature — mother concerned about growth and weight
144.caseSummary:
Differential: Hypopituitarism, Noonan syndrome.

The patient has Turner syndrome with coarctation of the aorta. Turner syndrome is a genetic abnormality (45,X genotype). Features include short stature, webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples, and shield chest. Coarctation of the aorta is common. Physical exam typically reveals a systolic murmur and differing systolic blood pressure between upper and lower extremities. Initial screening includes chest X-ray and ECG, with echocardiography as the gold standard for coarctation. Chromosome analysis (karyotype) confirms Turner syndrome. Management includes cardiothoracic surgery for coarctation and pediatric endocrinology for growth hormone therapy. Growth hormone levels are usually normal but not utilized correctly; estradiol replacement may be needed for ovarian failure.

Her mother reports she is the shortest girl in her class and is concerned about her growth. The patient has a good appetite and eats more than others her age; her mother is also worried about her weight. She is doing well in school, is active, and her mother has no other concerns. Born at term (40 weeks) via uncomplicated vaginal delivery; APGAR scores 10 and 10. No hospitalizations or medical problems. Vaccinations up to date. Family history is unremarkable.

145.chiefComplaint: Burning facial pain after shingles rash
145.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute herpes zoster, Painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy, Idiopathic painful trigeminal neuropathy.

The patient has Trigeminal Postherpetic Neuropathy. Cranial nerve V was injured during a herpes zoster outbreak. As the patient's pain started after a herpes zoster infection, the diagnosis is fairly straight forward. This case

does not require any imaging.

‘Once the diagnosis is made, the patient should be treated with medication. The cream that was prescribed by the urgent care was likely Capsaicin cream. The first line treatment for postherpetic neuralgia is
gabapentin/pregabalin. Tricyclics and antiseizure medications can be used as a secondary treatment. However, if these were ordered, points would be deducted. In this case, the patient will improve on medication treatment,

and the case will end.
145.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with persistent, severe, burning/shooting pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution (V1 most common) following a recent herpes zoster (shingles) outbreak with characteristic vesicular rash in the same distribution. Postherpetic neuralgia is the most common complication of HZ — pain persisting >90 days after rash resolution. Risk increases with age (>60). Caused by viral damage to sensory ganglia → neuropathic pain. Treatment: first-line — gabapentin or pregabalin, TCAs (amitriptyline, nortriptyline), lidocaine patch 5% (localized pain). Opioids NOT first-line. Prevention: recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for adults ≥50 — reduces HZ risk by >90% and PHN risk. VZV is reactivation of latent varicella virus in dorsal root ganglia.

146.title: Found Unconscious
146.chiefComplaint: Found unconscious, cherry-red skin, metabolic acidosis
146.caseSummary:
Differential: Carbon monoxide poisoning, Hydrogen sulfide gas poisoning, Phosphine poisoning
The patient has cyanide poisoning. The most common cause of cyanide poisoning in the United States is due to inhalation of smoke in residential or commercial fires. Cyanide disrupts the electron transport chain in the

mitochondrial production of ATP by binding to and inhibiting cytochrome oxidase a. As aerobic cellular metabolism stops, cells are forced into anerobic metabolism with the subsequent generation of lactate. This will cause
severe acidosis and very elevated lactate levels which can lead to cellular death.

Cyanide is produced in house fires due to combustion of materials such as rubber, wool, plastics, and synthetic materials.
The history suggests either a carbon monoxide poisoning or a cyanide poisoning. The hint in the history is that there is a dense acrid smoke that was protruding from the house. The patient will need to be intubated and put
‘ona ventilator. A fingerstick glucose, a CMP, an EKG, lactate, ABG, carboxyhemoglobin should be drawn, Lactate aids in differentiating between cyanide poisoning and carbon monoxide poisoning. If lactate is normal or mildly
elevated, then this would be more consistent with carbon monoxide poisoning alone.

As the carboxyhemoglobin is only 10%, along with severe acidosis and highly elevated lactate, the diagnosis of cyanide poisoning should be clear. The treatment of choice is Hydroxocobalamin. Hydroxocobalamin is the
hydroxylated active form of vitamin B12. Once Cyanide poisoning is suspected, an initial dose of Hydroxocobalamin should be given. If the patient does not quickly improve, then a second dose can be given. If the patient

does not improve then a third dose can be given along with sodium thiosulfate. Amyl/sodium Nitrite should be avoided as this can cause worsening oxygen delivery if the patient has concurrent carbon monoxide toxicity.

‘Once the patient is put on Hydroxocobalamin, the patient will begin to improve, and the case will end.

Sources: smoke inhalation (burning plastics/wool), industrial exposure, sodium nitroprusside infusion. Treatment: hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit — first-line, binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin which is renally excreted). Alternative: sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulfate (older regimen, risk of methemoglobinemia). Supportive: 100% oxygen, airway management, IVF, vasopressors if needed. Admit to ICU.

148.chiefComplaint: Pleuritic chest pain, fever weeks after MI
148.caseSummary:
Differential: Myocardial infarction, Myocardial Ischemia, Peptic Ulcer Disease, Pulmonary embolism, Aortic Dissection, Aortic stenosis, Esophageal Rupture, Esophageal Spasm, Acute gastritis, GERD, Coronary artery
vasospasm, Angina Pectoris, Esophagitis, Cardiac tamponade.

This case is similar to case #15. However, there are important differences. The main difference is to avoid treament with NSAIDS (not including Aspirin) as this should be avoided in Post Myocardial Infarction Pericarditis.

Acetaminophen or Aspirin can be given to help with the pain, but the pericarditis is typically self-limited and should resolve within in a week.
Diagnostics should focus on making sure that the patient is not having another myocardial infarction. Once this is ruled out, the patient can be treated for Post Myocardial Infarction Pericarditis.

The medications he is currently taking for his recent myocardial infarction (atenolol, clopidogrel, atorvastatin) should not be discontinued. Treatment with Colchicine is controversial in Post Myocardial Infarction Pericarditis as
there are not many studies showing its effectiveness, so this is optional.

As in case #15, the important aspect of this case is to not over-treat and not to do any invasive testing and/or treatment.
148.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with pleuritic chest pain, fever, malaise, and pericardial friction rub 2-6 weeks after a myocardial infarction. Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune-mediated pericarditis occurring post-MI (or post-cardiac surgery) — immune response to exposed myocardial antigens. ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression (pericarditis pattern). Echo: pericardial effusion (usually small). Differentiate from peri-infarct pericarditis (occurs within days of MI, localized ECG changes over infarct zone, more directly due to transmural necrosis). Treatment: high-dose aspirin (650mg q4-6h) or NSAIDs (ibuprofen). Colchicine added for symptom reduction and recurrence prevention. Avoid steroids unless refractory (impair myocardial healing). NOT heparin (risk of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion/tamponade).

Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune-mediated pericarditis occurring post-MI (or post-cardiac surgery) — immune response to exposed myocardial antigens. ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression (pericarditis pattern). Echo: pericardial effusion (usually small). Differentiate from peri-infarct pericarditis (occurs within days of MI, localized ECG changes over infarct zone, more directly due to transmural necrosis). Treatment: high-dose aspirin (650mg q4-6h) or NSAIDs (ibuprofen). Colchicine added for symptom reduction and recurrence prevention. Avoid steroids unless refractory (impair myocardial healing). NOT heparin (risk of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion/tamponade).

149.title: Chronic Diarrhea
149.chiefComplaint: Severe PUD, chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain
149.caseSummary:
Differential: Antral G-cell hyperplasia, Retained gastric antrum, Gastric outlet obstruction, Renal failure, idiopathic gastroesophageal reflux, peptic ulcer disease, Helicobacter pylori infection.

The patient has Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome which is caused by a gastrin secreting tumor located in the duodenum or pancreas. Men are more likely to be diagnosed with Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome than women. Most of

these tumors occur spontaneously, but some come from those with MEN type | (Multiple endocrine neoplasia type I).

Diarrhea is one of the most common symptoms of Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome. Excess gastrin concentrations inhibit the absorption of water and sodium by the small intestine which causes diarrhea. Other common symptoms
of Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome are: abdominal pain, heartburn, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, and bleeding.

A serum gastrin value greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal (1000 pg/ml) is diagnostic of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. The patient in this case has gastrin levels of 1,200 pg/mL.

An upper-Gl should be done to look for the tumor and to get a biopsy sample. A CT scan can be done to look for metastasis as gastrinomas can be malignant. Surgery should be consulted to remove the gastrinoma as

spontaneous gastrinomas can be cured by surgical removal of the tumor. The patient should be started on a PPI (ie. omeprazole) to limit complications of peptic ulcer disease.

‘Once the tumor is removed, the patient should be followed up by routine CT scans to check for any further occurrences. Screenings for parathormone levels, ionized calcium levels, and prolactin levels should be done to
screen for MEN1 tumors. The patient should also be counseled to stop smoking.
149.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe, refractory peptic ulcer disease, chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and GI bleeding. Multiple ulcers in atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). ZES is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma) — most commonly in the duodenum or pancreas → massive gastric acid hypersecretion → severe PUD and diarrhea (acid inactivates pancreatic enzymes + damages mucosa). Often associated with MEN1. Diagnosis: fasting serum gastrin level — markedly elevated (>1000 pg/mL or >10x normal). If borderline → secretin stimulation test (paradoxical increase in gastrin in ZES). Localize tumor: somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (Octreoscan), CT/MRI, EUS. Treatment: high-dose PPI (omeprazole, pantoprazole) to control acid hypersecretion. Surgical resection if localized. If metastatic or unresectable → long-term PPI + octreotide.

150.title: Back Pain and Fatigue
150.caseSummary:
Differential: Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia, Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance, Solitary Plasmacytoma,

The patient has Multiple Myeloma (MM). MM is a neoplastic proliferation of a single plasma cell line that produces monoclonal antibodies. This leads to large amounts of copies of one specific immunoglobulin (typically
either IgG or IgA). MM is twice a common in African-Americans than in Caucasians. The etiology of MM is unknown. The disease will progress as the normal bone marrow elements are replaced by malignant plasma cells.

The diagnosis of MM is made by a bone marrow biopsy showing at least 10% abnormal plasma cells plus one of the following: Bone lesions (as seen in this patient), renal insufficiency (with a creatinine greater than 2 mg/dL),
hypercalcemia, or anemia. The mnemonic of CRAB can be used to show the most common clinical manifestations of MM: C: hypercalcemia R: renal failure A: anemia B: bone disease.

Urinalysis will be negative. The dipsticks will be unable to detect Bence Jones protein, Serum/Urine immunofixation and serum free light chain assays are not current orders on the USMLE.
The prognosis for MM is typically poor. This is a diagnosis case, and treatment is to simply consult oncology, give bisphosphonates, and give fluids. Other treatments are outside the scope of the USMLE. The treatments

‘outside the scope of the USMLE would include autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation, Melphalan, dexamethasone, thalidomide, Ixazomib, Doxorubicin, and others.
150.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with persistent back pain (pathologic vertebral compression fractures), fatigue (normocytic anemia), and possibly hypercalcemia. Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells in bone marrow → monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein) production. Classic CRAB criteria: hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions (lytic lesions on X-ray/skeletal survey). Labs: elevated total protein with globulin gap, M spike on SPEP, immunofixation confirms monoclonal Ig (IgG most common), elevated kappa/lambda free light chains with abnormal ratio, Bence Jones protein in urine (UPEP). Bone marrow biopsy: >10% clonal plasma cells. Skeletal survey: lytic punched-out lesions. Treatment: induction (bortezomib + lenalidomide + dexamethasone), +/- autologous stem cell transplant if eligible. Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) for bone disease.

151.title: Found Unconscious
151.caseSummary:
Differential: Cyanide poisoning, Hydrogen sulfide gas poisoning, Phosphine poisoning

The patient has carbon monoxide poisoning. The most common cause of carbon monoxide poisoning in the United States is due to inhalation of fire-related smoke. Carbon Monoxide causes its detrimental effects by binding
to the iron moiety of heme. This binding changes the hemoglobin and greatly decreased the effectiveness of delivering oxygen to tissues.

Lactate aids in differentiating between cyanide poisoning and carbon monoxide poisoning. If lactate is normal or mildly elevated, then this would be more consistent with carbon monoxide poisoning alone.

‘An EKG should be done to check for cardiac ischemia as this can occur in carbon monoxide poisoning. A pregnancy test should be done as pregnancy can change treatment. Note that a pulse oximeter will be normal as a
pulse oximeter cannot tell the difference between carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin.

The patient should be immediately intubated and ventilated and started on 100% oxygen. Hyperbaric oxygen should be done in a patient if the patient has one of the following: COHb > 25%, COHb > 20% if the patient is
pregnant, unconscious; cardiac/neurologic ischemia; severe metabolic acidosis of pH < 7.1.

After treatment, the patient will improve and the case will end.
151.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious in an enclosed space with possible exposure (car exhaust, faulty heater, fire). Cherry-red skin, headache, confusion, nausea. CO binds hemoglobin with 240x affinity of O2 → carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) → impaired O2 delivery + cellular toxicity (binds cytochrome c oxidase). Pulse oximetry falsely NORMAL (cannot distinguish COHb from O2Hb). ABG: normal PaO2, elevated COHb (>3% nonsmokers, >10% smokers). Treatment: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather (reduces COHb half-life from 5h to 1h). Hyperbaric O2 if: COHb >25%, LOC, neurologic symptoms, cardiac ischemia, pregnancy. Monitor for delayed neurologic sequelae. Identify source — others at risk.

153.title: Skin Lesions
153.chiefComplaint: Fragile, blistering skin on sun-exposed areas
153.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute intermittent porphyria, Variegate porphyria, Hereditary coproporphyria, Congenital erythropoietic porphyria, Erythropoietic protoporphyria, X-linked protoporphyria, ALA dehydratase porphyria, Liver
disease

The patient in this case has Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT). PCT is caused due to reduce activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity leads to hepatic accumulation of
highly carboxylated porphyrinogens which are then transported to the skin which then cause damage when exposed to light. The light (near 400nm) activate oxygen in the tissues that damages proteins, basement
membranes, and lipids which causes the skin lesions and blistering.

Biopsies are not necessary in PCT. The diagnosis can be made through laboratory studies and clinical symptoms.

There are a variety of porphyrias that are on the differential. For the scope of the USMLE, the main differential to rule out is Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). PCT will have normal urine delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) levels

and normal porphobilinogen (PBG) levels while AIP will have elevated ALA and PBG levels. AIP will also have a port-wine color urine and can have recurrent bouts of severe abdominal pain.

A common cause of PCT is infection with the Hepatitis C virus. Although the patient has mildly elevated LFTs, the patient should be treated for Hepatitis C. This can be done by referring to infectious disease. The treatment
protocol for treating Hepatitis C is outside the scope of the USMLE, so an infectious disease referral is sufficient.

The treatment for PCT is Phlebotomy or low-dose hydroxychloroquine (or chloroquine). As sunlight is a factor that causes the blistering, the patient should be advised to avoid exposure to sunlight until porphyrin levels have

normalized. The patient should also be advised to avoid alcohol as this can exacerbate PCT.

In real life, it can take up to 6 months to get normal porphyrin concentrations with treatment. In this case, the patient will improve after a couple weeks of treatment.

154.title: Vaginal Discharge
154.caseSummary:
Differential: Atrophic Vaginitis, Purulent Vaginitis, Gonorrhea, Chlamydia, Bacterial vaginosis, Vulvovaginal candidiasis

The patient has a Trichomonal infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. Trichomoniasis is the most common non-viral sexually transmitted infection worldwide. Females are more likely to have Trichomoniasis
than males. The patient most likely got infected with Trichomonas vaginalis from her new sexual partner. The sexual partner should be treated for Trichomonas and confirmation of an Trichomonal infection in the sexual

partner is not required. The sexual partner should be given a single 2g dose of metronidazole.

The best way to diagnosis Trichomonas is to prepare a cervical wet mount and see the Trichomonas vaginalis moving on the slide under a microscope. Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) can also be done to diagnose, but

‘a wet mount is cheaper and more available.
The treatment of choice for a Trichomonal infection is metronidazole due to cost and availability. Tinidazole and Secnidazole (not currently an order on the USMLE) can also be used.
The patient should be screened for other sexually transmitted infections which include gonorrhea, chlamydia, and HIV. The patient should be counseled to avoid intercourse until the patient and their sexual partner are

asymptomatic and have completed treatment.

Diagnosis: wet mount shows motile trichomonads (flagellated organisms). Vaginal pH >4.5. Whiff test may be positive. NAAT (PCR) is gold standard — more sensitive than wet mount. Treatment: metronidazole 2g PO once or tinidazole 2g PO once. Treat sexual partners (even if asymptomatic). Avoid alcohol during treatment and for 24h after metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction). Screen for other STIs.

156.title: Generalized Swelling
156.chiefComplaint: Generalized edema, frothy urine, weight gain
156.caseSummary:
Differential: Heart Failure, Hereditary Angioedema, Kwashiorkor, Liver Cirrhosis.

The patient has Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome which is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children less than 10 years old. An official diagnosis can be made by doing a kidney biopsy and doing an electron
microscopy which would show diffuse foot process effacement. However, biopsy is not necessary as a diagnosis can be made based on the clinical presentation and lab findings (high proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia).

Edema from nephrotic syndrome is caused due to damage to the glomerular filtration barrier which increases permeability which leads to edema. Most patients with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome have minimal change
disease which is typically responsive to steroid treatment.

Evaluation of nephrotic syndrome would include urinalysis to look for proteinuria, 24 hour urine protein excretion study, Lipid panel, electrolytes, complete blood count, and complement studies.

Treatment of nephrotic syndrome is steroid therapy. Empiric steroid treatment can be started which is typically oral prednisone, but prednisolone can also be used. Diuretics should only be used for patients with severe

edema such as those with pleural effusions and/or ascites.

Although the patient has dyslipidemia, a course of steroid treatment should be undertaken, and the patient should be monitored before any intervention is pursued.

156.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with generalized edema (periorbital — worse in morning, then leg/scrotal), weight gain, frothy urine (proteinuria), and fatigue. Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria (>3.5g/day or >40mg/m2/hr in children), hypoalbuminemia (<2.5), edema, hyperlipidemia. Most common cause in children: minimal change disease (MCD) — 80-90%. Often preceded by viral URI. Diagnosis: UA — 3-4+ protein, oval fat bodies. 24h urine protein confirms nephrotic range. Renal biopsy NOT routinely needed in children (MCD most common and responds to steroids). Treatment: prednisone 2mg/kg/day (response = remission in 2-4 weeks confirms MCD). Salt/fluid restriction. Diuretics for severe edema. If steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing: consider biopsy, alternative immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine). Vaccinate before immunosuppression (pneumococcal). Monitor for complications: infection (loss of immunoglobulins), thrombosis (loss of antithrombin III).

157.title: Frequency of Urination
157.caseSummary:
Differential: Primary polydipsia, Central diabetes insipidus, Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, Hypernatremia

The patient has type Il Diabetes Mellitus. This is a very straight-forward case. The most common cause of polydipsia and polyuria is uncontrolled diabetes. A random blood glucose would be elevated along with a HgAtc. The

UA would have glucosuria with no proteinuria.

Typically, Metformin would be the initial medication of choice for a newly diagnosed Diabetes Mellitus type II without kidney or cardiovascular problems. However, the patient has a very high A1c (above 9%) as well as being

symptomatic. This will mean that the patient will unlikely be able to be successfully treated with Metformin treatment alone. The patient will need either insulin or a GLP-1 receptor agonist (Liraglutide, Dulaglutide,
semaglutide). Note Liraglutide and Dulaglutide are the only GLP-1 receptor agonist available on the USMLE. Other GLP-1 receptor agonists are not yet available.

If the patient has a lower A1c then Metformin could be sufficient. However, newer studies are showing that more newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus type Il patients are requiring insulin and GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment

at diagnosis. Therefore, if you start Metformin, and the patient improves only slightly, then you should immediately go to insulin or a GLP-1 receptor agonist such as liraglutide, semaglutide, or dulaglutide to treat the patient.

For preventive care, the patient should be advised to lose weight and exercise as this can help with glucose control.
157.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with polyuria (dilute urine), polydipsia (excessive thirst), nocturia, and hypernatremia. Central DI: deficiency of ADH (vasopressin) from posterior pituitary → inability to concentrate urine. Nephrogenic DI: kidneys resistant to ADH (lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia). Workup: 24h urine volume (>3L/day), urine osmolality (<300 despite hypernatremia), serum osmolality elevated, hypernatremia. Water deprivation test: cannot concentrate urine despite fluid restriction. After desmopressin (DDAVP): central DI = urine osmolality increases >50% (kidneys respond to exogenous ADH). Nephrogenic DI = no response. Treatment: central DI → desmopressin (DDAVP) intranasal or PO. Nephrogenic → treat underlying cause, thiazide diuretics (paradoxically reduce urine output), low-solute diet. Free water access essential.

159.title: Abnormal Behavior
159.chiefComplaint: Elevated mood, decreased sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity
159.caseSummary:
Differential: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features, Stimulant intoxication, Schizophrenia, Borderline personality disorder.
The patient has newly onset bipolar disorder. As the patient had a full manic episode, the patient will be classified as Bipolar |. A single manic episode is enough to qualify for Bipolar | as long as it was not caused by
substances, medications, or any other external factors. To make a diagnosis of a manic episode, you can use the DIG FAST mnemonic. D = Distractibility, | = Indiscretion (increased risky behaviors), G = Grandiosity, F= Flight of

Ideas, A = Increased Activity, S = Sleep deficit, T = Talkativeness.

Three of the DIGFAST symptoms need to be met to have a diagnosis of mania if the patient has euphoric mood (4 if the patient is irritable). The patient has been involved in risky-behavior, talking fast; has increased goal
directed activity such as creating business plans; grandiosity, thinking she is creating companies that will revolutionize the world; and has a decreased need for sleep.

The treatment for a first-time manic episode in a newly onset bipolar patient is a mood stabilizer (mainly lithium or valproate) along with an antipsychotic. Lithium is likely to better choice in this patient as valproate can be
problematic for patients of childbearing age. However, itis still technically correct to use valproate in an acutely manic patient, so credit will be given.

The antipsychotic could be any first- or second-generation antipsychotic. Common antipsychotics used is haloperidol, aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, or risperidone. Psychiatry should be consulted. Perhaps in the future,
the patient can be maintained on monotherapy of either a mood stabilizer or an antipsychotic, but during this acute manic period, the patient should be started on both.

After a couple days, the patient's mania will subside, and the case will end. The patient should be counseled about safe sex practices, medication compliance, and against heavy alcohol use.

160.title: Anxiety
160.chiefComplaint: Excessive worry for months, restlessness, sleep problems
160.caseSummary:
Differential: Panic Disorder, Adjustment Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder.

The patient has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The patient experienced a traumatic event of being stabbed during a robbery. The diagnosis of PTSD requires the following (from the DSM-5):
Criterion A. Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence in one (or more) of the following ways:

1. Directly experiencing the traumatic event(s).
2. Witnessing, in person, the event(s) as it occurred to others.

3. Learning that the traumatic event(s) occurred to a close family member or close friend. In cases of actual or threatened death of a family member or friend, the event(s) must have been violent or accidental.

4, Experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of the traumatic event(s) (e.g,, first responders collecting human remains; police officers repeatedly exposed to details of child abuse). Note: Criterion A4
does not apply to exposure through electronic media, television, movies, or pictures, unless this exposure is work related.

Criterion B: Presence of one (or more) of the following intrusion symptoms associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning after the traumatic event(s) occurred:
1. Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event(s). Note: In children older than 6 years, repetitive play may occur in which themes or aspects of the traumatic event(s) are expressed.

2. _ Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event(s). Note: In children, there may be frightening dreams without recognizable content.

3. Dissociative reactions (e.g,, flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event(s) were recurring. (Such reactions may occur on a continuum, with the most extreme expression being a complete loss
of awareness of present surroundings.) Note: In children, trauma-specific reenactment may occur in play.

4, _ Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event(s).

5. Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event(s).

Criterion C:
Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by one or both of the following:

1. Avoidance of or efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event(s).

2. Avoidance of or efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic
event(s).

Criterion D:
Negative alterations in cognitions and mood associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning or worsening after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by two (or more) of the following:

1. _ Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event(s) (typically due to dissociative amnesia, and not to other factors such as head injury, alcohol, or drugs).

2. Persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs or expectations about oneself, others, or the world (eg, “I am bad,” “No one can be trusted,” “The world is completely dangerous,” “My whole nervous system is permanently
ruined’).

3. Persistent, distorted cognitions about the cause or consequences of the traumatic event(s) that lead the individual to blame himself/herself or others.

4, Persistent negative emotional state (e.g,, fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame).

5. Markedly diminished interest or participation in significant activities.

6. Feelings of detachment or estrangement from others.

7. _ Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g,, inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).

Criterion E:
Marked alterations in arousal and reactivity associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning or worsening after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by two (or more) of the following:
Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation), typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression toward people or objects.

Reckless or self-destructive behavior.

Hypervigilance.

Exaggerated startle response.

Problems with concentration.

ae wN >

Sleep disturbance (e.g,, difficulty falling or staying asleep or restless sleep).

Criterion F. Duration of the disturbance (Criteria B, C, D and E) is more than 1 month.

Criterion G: The disturbance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

Criterion H: The disturbance is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., medication, alcohol) or another medical condition.

This is a lot to remember. Try to remember the core features of PTSD which are changes to affect or behavior after a traumatic event that cause impairment in day-to-day life. Typical symptoms would be avoidant behaviors
with anxiety/depression, flashbacks, nightmares, and hypervigilance.

The patient in this case meets all the criteria for PTSD with having a traumatic experience and then having flashbacks, avoiding going out at night, being fearful and anxious, not spending time with family, feeling irritable,
having nightmares, and having hypervigilance. These symptoms are affecting his life as he is calling in sick to work.

The treatment for PTSD is mainly psychotherapy but SSRI/SNRIs can also be used if the patient does not wish to participate in psychotherapy. We recommend that for the USMLE, both psychotherapy and
psychopharmacology be offered to the patient as some studies show slightly increased favorable outcomes when combining psychopharmacology with psychotherapy.

‘SSRis/SNRis that are typically started for PTSD would be Paxil, Zoloft/Fluvoxamine, Fluoxetine, Celexa, Lexapro, Effexor, Cymbalta.
Evidence based psychotherapy for PTSD include: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), Cognitive processing therapy (CPT), Prolonged exposure therapy (CPT), and Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR). All
these types of therapy are evidence based. The specifics of what is done in each of these therapies is outside the scope of the USMLE. The USMLE only has Cognitive Behavioral Therapy as an order which is translated as

simply a referral to Psychiatry or Psychology.

‘Some treatment can take months for improvement with PTSD symptoms. As this is early in the diagnosis, early intervention can result in more rapid improvement. The patient will improve after two weeks of treatment and
will be close to symptom free after 4 weeks of treatment. This is an ideal case and an ideal response.

161.title: Headache
161.caseSummary:
Differential: Thyrotoxicosis, Panic attacks, Illegal drug ingestion, Carcinoid syndrome, Essential hypertension, Hypoglycemia, Migraines

The patient in this case has a Pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytomas will secrete Catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine). She has a 6 cm right adrenal mass which has been causing the patient's
symptoms of high blood pressure, headache, panic attack like symptoms, sweating, and dizziness. The majority of patients with pheochromocytoma will have headache as a symptom.

The way to diagnose pheochromocytoma is to measure the urine catecholamines and/or fractionated metanephrines. Once these come back elevated, imaging should be done to find the location of the pheochromocytoma.
The imaging choice is either CT or MRI of the abdomen/pelvis.

The patient's high blood pressure should be addressed. Phenoxybenzamine should be started which is a nonspecific, long-acting alpha-adrenergic blocking agent. This is ideal for preoperatively treating to normalize blood

pressure. Alternatives to Phenoxybenzamine are prazosin, terazosin, or doxazosin.

A beta blocker, particularly propranolol or metoprolol, should be started. It is very important to start this AFTER the alpha blocker is started to prevent unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation which could dangerously
increase the patient's blood pressure.

Surgery should be consulted to remove the patient's tumor. Once surgery is consulted, the case will end.
161.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with episodic severe headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis (classic triad), and paroxysmal hypertension. Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells. Rule of 10's: 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma), 10% malignant, 10% familial (MEN2, VHL, NF1). Diagnosis: plasma free metanephrines or 24h urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (elevated). CT/MRI abdomen — adrenal mass. Pre-operative alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) BEFORE beta-blockade (beta-blockade alone → unopposed alpha agonism → hypertensive crisis). Adequate alpha blockade for 10-14 days before surgery. Then add beta-blocker if tachycardia. Surgical resection (adrenalectomy) is curative.

162.title: Pain During Urination
162.caseSummary:
Differential: Pelvic inflammatory disease, Urethritis, Vaginitis

The patient in this case has acute cystitis. This is a very common ailment in women due to the close proximity of women's urethra to the anus. This is a simple case of acute cystitis with the typical symptoms of dysuria, urinary

frequency, and urinary urgency. This would mean that the infection is confined to the bladder.

If the patient had fevers, chills, flank pain, or other symptoms of systemic infection, then you would suspect infection outside of the bladder. If this were the case, then pyelonephritis and complicated urinary tract infections

would be high on the differential.

This case is different than case #24 because in case #24, the patient is pregnant. A urinalysis should be done. When it comes back positive, the patient should be started on antibiotics.

First line antibiotics are Nitrofurantoin, Trimethoprim with or without sulfamethoxazole, and Fosfomycin.

Second line agents for acute cystitis are beta-lactams (Amoxicillin-clavulanate, Cefpodoxime, Cefdinir, Cefadroxil, Cephalexin). Points would be lost for using a second line agent for this simple case of acute cystitis

Third agents for acute cystitis are fluroquinolones (i. Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin). These should be reserved for only serious cases. This would be inappropriate in a simple acute cystitis case. More points would be lost for

using fluroquinolones in this case.

Preventive care of a pap smear should be offered to the patient.
162.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and no vaginal discharge or irritation. No systemic symptoms (fever, CVA tenderness → rules out pyelo). Uncomplicated UTI in healthy premenopausal non-pregnant woman. Most common: E. coli (80%). Diagnosis: UA — positive leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria, bacteriuria. Urine culture not routinely needed for uncomplicated cystitis (treat empirically). Treatment: nitrofurantoin 100mg PO BID x 5d (first-line), TMP-SMX DS PO BID x 3d (if local resistance <20%), fosfomycin 3g PO once. Avoid fluoroquinolones for uncomplicated cystitis (FDA warnings). Counsel: void after intercourse, adequate hydration, cranberry products (limited evidence). If recurrent → postcoital or continuous prophylaxis.
