163.chiefComplaint: Ear pain, fever, pulling at ear
163.caseSummary:
Differential: Otitis Externa, Ear Trauma, Foreign Body

The patient in this case has Acute Otitis Media. This is a very common ailment in children which is caused by a bacterial infection in the middle ear fluid. The most common presentation is ear pain and hearing loss. The
classical physical exam finding on exam is a bulging tympanic membrane. The bulging happens when there is middle ear effusion and inflammation which pushes the tympanic membrane.

This is mainly a treatment case as the main required diagnostic order is a HEENT physical exam.
First line treatment for otitis media in children is Amoxicillin or Amoxicillin/Clavulanate.

Second line treatments for otitis media in children are: Cefdinir, Cefpoxime, Cefuroxime, Ceftriaxone, Azithromycin, Clarithromycin, Clindamycin, and Levofloxacin. These are not ideal for a simple case of otitis media and
points would be lost if these antibiotics were chosen,

The patient should be given acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain, and the patient should be counseled about medication compliance to complete the entire antibiotic regimen to avoid antibiotic resistance and reinfection.

164.title: Pelvic Pain
164.chiefComplaint: Acute severe unilateral pelvic pain, nausea
164.caseSummary:
Differential: Ectopic Pregnancy, Tubo-Ovarian Abscess, Appendicitis, Kidney Stones, Ruptured Ovarian Cyst.

The patient in this case has Ovarian Torsion. This is a relatively rare surgical emergency. The most common presentation is pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting. A pelvic mass is a risk factor for ovarian torsion (i. cyst,

dermoid). The patient has a 7cm cyst with decrease blood flow.

Ovarian torsion is caused by rotation of the infundibulopelvic ligament which restricts blood flow causing pain and eventually necrosis if surgical intervention is not quickly performed. The treatment for ovarian torsion is

surgical detorsion (assuming the ovary is not necrotic).

The patient's symptoms of having cramping over the last few days was likely due to the ovary twisting and untwisting repeatedly.

OB/GYN should be consulted for a laparoscopic detorsion.

Pain is sudden, severe, and may have occurred intermittently before (partial torsion). Ovarian torsion is a GYNECOLOGIC EMERGENCY — the ovary twists on its vascular pedicle → venous and lymphatic outflow obstruction → arterial compromise → ovarian ischemia and necrosis if not detorsed within hours. Risk: ovarian mass/cyst, pregnancy, ovulation induction. Diagnosis: pelvic ultrasound with Doppler — enlarged ovary, decreased/absent arterial and venous flow. However, normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion (may be intermittent or only venous flow absent). Treatment: EMERGENCY surgical exploration with detorsion (preserve ovary if viable) ± oophoropexy. Do NOT delay surgery for imaging if high clinical suspicion.

165.title: Postcoital Bleeding
165.caseSummary:
Differential: Cervicitis, Vaginitis, Vaginal Cancer, Cervical Poly, Endometriosis
The patient in this case has Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) of the cervix. SCC is the most common type of cervical cancer in the United States. The majority of cases are due to Human papillomavirus (HPV) infections acquired
years before. The history mentions that the patient has been treated for chlamydia 20 years ago. It is assumed that the patient (or partner) was having multiple sexual partners and likely acquired HPV at this time which slowly

led to cervical neoplasia over time.

The pelvic exam will show a visible cervical lesion which should be biopsied which will return with SCC of the cervix. The patient will most likely require a hysterectomy, so OB/GYN should be consulted along with oncology.
SCC is typically sensitive to chemotherapy, so this consult should be offered,

166.title: Easy Bruising / Bleeding
166.chiefComplaint: Joint bleeding, easy bruising, prolonged PTT
166.caseSummary:
Differential: von Willebrand's disease, Platelet Disorder, Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation, Factor XI deficiency, Factor XIll deficiency, Vitamin K deficiency

The patient in this case has Hemophilia A. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder which mostly affects males. The family history of the patient's mother's brother having a “bleeding disorder” is relevant. Hemophilia A
is caused by a deficiency of factor Vill. Hemophilia B is a deficiency of Factor IX and Hemophilia C is a deficiency of factor XI.

Some patients with Hemophilia can go undetected for years until an event such as trauma, surgical interventions, or dental extractions. The treatment is simple, you replace what is deficient, so in this case, you give Factor VIII
therapy, and the bleeding will stop.

The patient should be offered genetic counseling with parents and the patient should be reassured.
166.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with excessive bleeding after minor trauma, easy bruising, hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints — knees, ankles, elbows), and prolonged PTT with normal PT and normal platelet count. Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII. Severity: mild (5-40% FVIII), moderate (1-5%), severe (<1%). PTT is prolonged (intrinsic pathway), PT normal (extrinsic pathway intact), platelets normal. Mixing study: PTT corrects (rules out inhibitor). Factor VIII assay confirms low activity. Treatment: factor VIII concentrate (recombinant preferred) for bleeding episodes or prophylaxis. Desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild hemophilia A (releases stored VIII and vWF). Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, IM injections. Genetic counseling (X-linked).

167.title: Nausea and Vomiting
167.chiefComplaint: Chronic nausea, vomiting undigested food hours later
167.caseSummary:
Differential: Bowel Obstruction, Functional dyspepsia, Bulimia
The patient in this case has Diabetic Gastroparesis. This is caused by diabetic neuropathy of the autonomic system causing decreased motility of the stomach. This can happen in both type | and type II diabetes.

First line treatment for gastroparesis is Metoclopramide. Metoclopramide (Reglan) is both an antiemetic and a prokinetic and is FDA approved to treat gastroparesis for up to 12 weeks (This can be longer if the patient is
willing to take on the risks of tardive dyskinesia).

Metoclopramide is a D2 blocker, so it comes with the risk of tardive dyskinesia (this is like taking haloperidol for an extended period of time). Domperidone is used in the UK and Canada, but this is not available in the US and
is not an order on the USMLE.

Second line treatment for gastroparesis is Erythromycin or Azithromycin. Both of these antibiotics increase gastric emptying.

The patient's increased glucose should be treated. The patient should be put on insulin therapy due to the frequent vomiting. It is unlikely he is getting much efficacy from oral medications. He can be trialed to be
transitioned back to oral medications once his nausea and vorniting is controlled.

Glucose control can help gastroparesis symptoms, but the damage done by prolonged hyperglycemia could be a permanent issue for the patient. However, glucose control should be implemented regardless.

In this case, the patient will feel better after given Metoclopramide.
167.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a diabetic patient presenting with chronic nausea, vomiting of undigested food eaten hours earlier, early satiety, bloating, and erratic blood glucose control. Diabetic gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying due to autonomic neuropathy — vagus nerve damage from chronic hyperglycemia. Diagnosis: gastric emptying study (scintigraphy) — delayed emptying of radiolabeled meal. Upper endoscopy to rule out obstruction. Treatment: glycemic control (most important). Dietary: small frequent meals, low-fiber, low-fat. Medications: prokinetics — metoclopramide (first-line, watch for EPS/tardive dyskinesia, limit to 12 weeks), erythromycin, domperidone. Antiemetics: ondansetron. Severe refractory: gastric electrical stimulator, jejunostomy tube.

168.title: Fatigue
168.chiefComplaint: Daytime sleepiness, loud snoring, witnessed apneas
168.caseSummary:
Differential: Central Sleep Apnea, Psychogenic Sleepiness, Sleep Deprivation, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, Deconditioning, Obesity Hypoventtilation Syndrome

The patient in this case has Obstructive Sleep Apnea; a common condition in obese patients. There is a lot going on with this patient. The point of this case is to screen for all of the complications of obesity. Common
complications of obesity include Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, Heart Disease, Hyperlipidemia, Sleep Apnea, Liver dysfunction, Osteoarthritis.

The pertinent labs to order would be @ CMP to look at liver enzymes and electrolytes, a CBC to look at hematocrit, a lipid panel to look at lipid status, and an A1c to check glucose control.
Fatigue is a vague symptom and could be a lot of things. Fatigue is a common symptom in obese patients and could be deconditioning. However, with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) being so common in obese patients, a
sleep study should be done which in this case will show OSA.

The treatment for OSA is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BPAP). The patient's diabetes should be treated with insulin to get it under control prior to surgery, and then the patient
can be transitioned back to oral medications.

The patient's blood pressure may come down with the treatment of CPAP, so it would be prudent to wait until follow-up prior to changing the patient's blood pressure medications. The case will end shortly after CPAP is

ordered. The patient should be recommended a low-calorie diet as this will be required even after the bariatric surgery.

169.title: Somnolence
169.caseSummary:
Differential: Hyperparathyroidism, Excessive Opioid use, Effects of Metastatic Cancer

Hypercalcemia is common in patients with metastatic cancer. The mechanism of hypercalcemia secondary to malignancy can be due to a number of factors. It could be due to the tumor secreting parathyroid hormone-
related protein, due to bone metastasis causing local release of cytokines causing release of calcium, or it could be due to the tumor production calcitriol. It could also be a combination of these factors.

The patient can be put in any location except the ICU as the patient does not wish for extreme intervention. The best first step is to get a PTH to see if it's is low. If itis low such as in this case, this means that it is being
suppressed by tumor producing parathyroid hormone-related protein.

The patient has somnolence due to severe hypercalcemia with a calcium level of 14. The treatment for severe hypercalcemia of malignancy is to treat with IV fluids, calcitonin, and a bisphosphonate. It will take several days for
‘the bisphosphonate to be effective (typically day 2-4).

After the first 48 hours, calcitonin should be stopped and the bisphosphonate should be continued. Calcitonin will stop being effective due to receptor downregulation, but it is the short-term treatment that can help
hypercalcemia while waiting for the longer acting bisphosphonate to start working.

The bisphosphonate of choice in hypercalcemia of malignancy is Zoledronic acid, but Pamidronate, Ibandronate, and other bisphosphonates can also be used.
169.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive somnolence, confusion, fatigue, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, and nausea. Labs: elevated calcium (>11), low PTH (rules out primary hyperparathyroidism), elevated PTHrP. Hypercalcemia of malignancy is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients. Mechanisms: PTHrP secretion (squamous cell cancers — lung, head/neck), osteolytic bone metastases (breast, multiple myeloma), excess 1,25-vitamin D (lymphoma). Treatment: aggressive IV normal saline (3-4L/day) to promote calciuresis. Then IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or pamidronate — inhibit osteoclast activity). Calcitonin for rapid short-term reduction. Denosumab if refractory. Treat underlying malignancy. Monitor for arrhythmias (shortened QT on ECG).

170.title: Fall
170.caseSummary:
Differential: Vasovagal syncope, Postprandial hypotension, Afferent baroreflex failure

The patient has a simple case of orthostatic hypotension secondary to dehydration. This is verified by a postural vital sign which turns out to be positive. The patient's Hydrochlorothiazide should be discontinued, and IV fluids

should be given.
That is pretty much all the intervention required. There are no orders on the USMLE to council the patient to increase fluid intake or to increase salt intake. Compression stockings are translated to anti-embolism stockings, so

these are not required. The patient improves with IV fluids so fludrocortisone is not required.
170.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with recurrent falls, dizziness, lightheadedness, and near-syncope upon standing (within 3 min of standing). Orthostatic hypotension = drop in SBP ≥20mmHg or DBP ≥10mmHg within 3 min of standing. Causes: medications (antihypertensives — especially alpha-blockers, diuretics, nitrates, TCAs, dopaminergics), hypovolemia, autonomic neuropathy (DM, Parkinson's), prolonged bed rest. Workup: orthostatic vital signs, medication review, CBC (anemia), BMP (dehydration, electrolyte), EKG, consider autonomic testing. Treatment: review and adjust medications. Non-pharmacologic: increase fluid/salt intake (if no CHF), compression stockings, elevate head of bed, slow position changes, avoid prolonged standing. If needed: fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid — expand volume) or midodrine (alpha-1 agonist).

172.title: Hanging
172.chiefComplaint: Attempted hanging, ligature marks on neck
172.caseSummary:
Differential: Complex suicide, Attempted Homicide
The patient has had a near hanging incident. The patient requires emergency care including cervical collar, intubation and ventilation, transfer to the ICU, neurosurgical consultation, and spinal surgery. Although this case the

patient has a cervical vertebra injury with cervical spinal cord impingement, this is very rare in real life. Most patients with near hangings will not have cervical spine injuries, but this does show up more commonly on tests, so

don’t be surprised if this unlikely event appears on the USMLE.
Treating spinal cord injuries and cerebral edema with corticosteroids is controversial. Itis still commonly used in most spinal cord injuries for medicolegal reasons, so it is recommended that this is still given.
The patient has both ischemic and hemorthagic pathology on the patient's head imaging. It is reasonable to allow the patient's blood pressure to remain elevated during the first 24 hours to allow reperfusion. Keeping blood

pressure below 180/105 for the first 24 hours is a reasonable goal.

Itis recommended that Salicylate, Acetaminophen, and Alcohol levels are drawn as this could be a complex suicide involving both drug overdose with hanging. Once the patient is stabilized, the patient will need to be
admitted to the inpatient psychiatry ward and started on psychiatric treatment.

173.title: Sexual Assault
173.caseSummary:
Differential: Alcohol intoxication, Traumatic injury, Syncopal episode, Hypoglycemia

This case is similar to cases of female rape, where a rape kit is critical for evidence collection, including bodily fluids and physical injuries. Anal swabs should be collected as part of the forensic examination. Social services
involvement is crucial for support and coordination with law enforcement.

HIV prophylaxis should be initiated as noted in the case. Follow-up testing for HIV is recommended at 1 month and 3 months post-assault. Empiric antibiotics should be given for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis.
This included ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and metronidazole (or tinidazole).

Psychiatry/psychology should be involved to follow-up with the patient to process the trauma that he has experienced.

The patient should be tested for Syphilis, An HPV vaccine should also be given to the patient as this could help the patient prevent HPV-cancers such as anal cancer that is more common in men who has sex with men.
173.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents after sexual assault. Management: trauma-informed, multidisciplinary approach. Medical stabilization first, then forensic examination with consent. SANE examination if available. Forensic evidence collection (rape kit) within 72h. Document injuries. Labs: STI testing (CT, GC, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C), toxicology if concern for drug-facilitated assault. Empiric STI prophylaxis: ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole. HIV PEP if exposure within 72h (28-day course). Hepatitis B vaccine if not immune. Mental health crisis counseling. Report to law enforcement (with patient consent). Safe discharge planning. Follow-up: STI re-testing, counseling.

174.title: Hematemesis
174.chiefComplaint: Hematemesis and melena in a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis
174.caseSummary:
Differential: Esophageal varices, peptic ulcer disease, Mallory-Weiss tear, gastric erosions, malignancy.
Esophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins that develop as a consequence of portal hypertension, most 
commonly from cirrhosis. As portal pressure increases, portosystemic collaterals form to decompress the 
portal system, including vessels in the esophagus and gastric fundus. These thin-walled varices are prone to 
rupture, causing life-threatening upper GI bleeding. Patients with cirrhosis often have concurrent 
coagulopathy (elevated INR from decreased clotting factor synthesis) and thrombocytopenia (from 
hypersplenism), which can worsen bleeding. This case presents a classic scenario: a 55-year-old man with 

alcoholic cirrhosis presenting with hematemesis and melena, found to have severe anemia (Hct 24%, Hgb 8.0), 
mild coagulopathy (INR 1.8), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 100,000).
The diagnosis begins with a focused physical examination assessing for signs of shock (tachycardia, 
hypotension), stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly), and confirming GI bleeding 
(rectal exam for melena). Essential laboratory testing includes CBC (to quantify anemia and 
thrombocytopenia), comprehensive metabolic panel or basic metabolic panel (elevated BUN/Cr ratio suggests 
upper GI bleed), liver function tests (confirm cirrhosis), and coagulation studies (PT/INR to assess synthetic 
function). An abdominal ultrasound can confirm cirrhosis with nodular liver contour, splenomegaly, and 
ascites. The definitive diagnosis is made via urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with band ligation, 
which is both diagnostic and therapeutic—this is the single most important intervention.
Acute management focuses on careful resuscitation and pharmacologic therapy to control bleeding. Type and 
crossmatch for blood products immediately. Provide IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline, but avoid over-
resuscitation as excessive volume can increase portal pressure and worsen bleeding. PRBC transfusion should 
follow a restrictive strategy, targeting hemoglobin 7-9 g/dL rather than aggressive transfusion, as over-
transfusion paradoxically increases rebleeding risk. With platelets at 100,000 and INR at 1.8, this patient does 
NOT require platelet or FFP transfusions—these would only be indicated if platelets <50,000 or significantly 
higher INR with active bleeding.
Octreotide IV is critical—this vasoactive drug causes splanchnic vasoconstriction, reducing portal pressure and 
bleeding. Alternatives include somatostatin, terlipressin (preferred in Europe), or vasopressin with nitroglycerin 
(rarely used). Antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone IV is essential in all cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding, as 
it prevents spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and reduces mortality by 10-15%. Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime are 
superior choices; quinolones (norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin) are acceptable but inferior due to rising resistance. PPI 
therapy with pantoprazole IV helps stabilize clots, though it's less critical in variceal bleeding than peptic ulcer 
disease. The patient should be made NPO to prepare for urgent endoscopy.
After acute stabilization, several preventive measures are crucial. Non-selective beta-blockers such as 
propranolol, nadolol, or carvedilol should be started for secondary prophylaxis against rebleeding once the 
patient is hemodynamically stable—these are NOT given during acute bleeding as they can worsen 
hypotension. Beta-blockers reduce portal pressure and significantly decrease rebleeding rates. Hepatitis A and 
B vaccination should be administered to all cirrhotic patients to prevent superinfection that could cause 
further hepatic decompensation. Finally, alcohol cessation counseling is essential to prevent progression of 
cirrhosis and reduce risk of future variceal hemorrhage. These preventive measures are implemented after the 
acute bleed is controlled and should be part of discharge planning.
Two medications commonly used in cirrhosis management warrant specific mention in this context. Lactulose 
should be initiated to prevent hepatic encephalopathy, a frequent and serious complication following upper 
GI bleeding in cirrhotic patients. Digested blood in the gut provides a large protein load, driving intestinal 
ammonia production; lactulose acidifies the colon to trap ammonia as ammonium (NH₄⁺) and accelerates gut 

transit to eliminate it. This is standard preventive care in any cirrhotic patient with significant GI bleeding, even 
in the absence of overt encephalopathy at presentation. Spironolactone, on the other hand, is an aldosterone 
antagonist diuretic commonly used for chronic ascites management in cirrhosis, typically in combination with 
furosemide. However, spironolactone is contraindicated during acute variceal hemorrhage — the patient is 
already volume-depleted and hemodynamically unstable, and administering a diuretic in this setting risks 
worsening hypotension and acute kidney injury. Spironolactone should only be considered after the acute 
bleed has been controlled and the patient is hemodynamically stable, if ascites management is required as 
part of ongoing outpatient cirrhosis care.

175.title: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
175.caseSummary:
Differential: Von Willebrand disease (vWD), Thrombocytopenia, Hemophilia A, Platelet Abnormalities (Glanzmann thrombasthenia), Vasculopathies, Connective Tissue Diseases, Collagen Disorders, hypothyroidism.

The first step is to assess anemia and platelet count by getting a CBC. This shows anemia but normal platelets. Then order PT/PTT, revealing normal PT, mildly elevated PTT, and normal fibrinogen, pointing toward vWD. This is a classic presentation for vWD diagnosis in females around menarche due to heavy periods. Once suspected, order vWF assays showing decreased ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation at 1.0 mg/mL, suggestive of type 1 vWD. Confirmatory vWF activity takes 3 days, so the case ends before results, but initial findings allow empirical treatment.

Start IV fluids for hypovolemia. Give DDAVP (desmopressin, 0.3 mcg/kg IV) concurrently with tranexamic acid for acute bleeding control. DDAVP boosts endogenous vWF/Factor VIII, working within 30-60 minutes (peak at 1 hour), lasting 8-24 hours. It's safe for type 1; risks include hyponatremia and tachyphylaxis. Avoid in type 2B as it may worsen thrombocytopenia. If ineffective, use vWF concentrates.

Tranexamic Acid is typically started concurrently with DDAVP, not after it fails, to stabilize clots and enhance hemostasis, especially for mucosal bleeding like menorrhagia.

Preventive care would be to prevent future bleeds, so hormonal therapy such as oral contraceptives could be started or the patient could be referred to OB/GYN. Hormonal therapy helps by increasing vWF/factor VIII levels and stabilizing the endometrium. Counsel the patient on avoiding NSAIDs and trauma (playing sports). Add iron for anemia.

181.title: Nocturnal Enuresis
181.diagnosis: Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Secondary Nocturnal Enuresis
181.chiefComplaint: Nocturnal enuresis, loud snoring, daytime fatigue
181.caseSummary:
Differential diagnosis: Primary nocturnal enuresis, secondary enuresis due to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), diabetes mellitus, urinary tract infection, constipation, neurogenic bladder, seizure disorder, psychosocial stressors.

This patient has severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) accompanied by secondary nocturnal enuresis. In children and adolescents, OSA is frequently caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy, which is often made worse by
obesity. The key clinical features of OSA in this age group include loud snoring every night, witnessed pauses in breathing (apneas), habitual mouth breathing, daytime sleepiness or fatigue, and behavioral problems such as
inattention and irritability that can mimic attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

The secondary enuresis occurs because OSA leads to nocturnal polyuria—triggered by negative intrathoracic pressure during obstructed breathing, release of atrial natriuretic peptide, and an elevated arousal threshold that
prevents the child from waking to a full bladder. Obesity further increases the risk by worsening upper airway collapsibility and serving as a major contributing factor.

The initial evaluation should include a urinalysis to rule out urinary tract infection or glucosuria as potential causes of the enuresis. Because prediabetes is common in obese patients with OSA, fasting glucose and/or HbA1c
should be checked. A lipid panel is also warranted to screen for dyslipidemia and features of metabolic syndrome.

The confirmatory diagnostic test is an overnight polysomnography (sleep study), which establishes the diagnosis of OSA and quantifies its severity. In pediatric patients, an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) greater than 10 events
per hour indicates severe OSA. In this case, the results show an AHI of 25-35 events per hour along with oxygen desaturations.

According to guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS), the first-line treatment for OSA associated with adenotonsillar
hypertrophy is adenotonsillectomy (surgical removal of the tonsils and adenoids), and referral to an otolaryngologist (ENT) is appropriate even in obese adolescents. This procedure typically leads to significant improvement
in the AHI, resolution of enuresis in many cases, and better behavior and quality of life. However, obesity raises the risk of residual OSA after surgery (persistence in approximately 40-60% of obese children), so aggressive
counseling on weight loss through dietary changes and increased physical activity is essential. This approach also helps manage the patient's prediabetes and dyslipidemia while reducing the likelihood of OSA recurrence.
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is considered a second-line option, reserved for cases of persistent OSA after adenotonsillectomy, when surgery is refused or contraindicated, or when adherence to other measures

is poor; however, long-term adherence to CPAP can be difficult in teenagers.

Enuresis-specific treatments, such as desmopressin or an enuresis alarm, should not be started initially. The underlying OSA should be treated first, because the bedwetting often resolves completely or substantially improves
after adenotonsillectomy. Similarly, referral to psychiatry or initiation of medications for presumed ADHD should be deferred until the OSA is addressed, as the behavioral symptoms frequently improve once sleep quality is

restored.
For preventive care, provide intensive lifestyle counseling with a realistic weight loss goal of 0.5~1 kg per week, achieved through a structured calorie deficit and increased daily activity. Prediabetes and dyslipidemia should be
managed primarily with diet and exercise; metformin is rarely used as first-line therapy in pediatric prediabetes unless there is clear progression toward type 2 diabetes. After adenotonsillectomy, schedule follow-up in 4-8

weeks to reassess symptoms, enuresis, and behavior. If symptoms persist, consider repeating polysomnography to evaluate for residual OSA.

‘Common pitfalls to avoid include ordering desmopressin at the outset (which only treats the symptom rather than the underlying cause), initiating CPAP as the primary therapy without first attempting adenotonsillectomy,
failing to screen for metabolic complications (prediabetes and dyslipidemia), or delaying referral to ENT.

v Review Later
181.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with primary or secondary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting), loud snoring, restless sleep, daytime fatigue, and behavioral issues. Severe OSA causes nocturnal enuresis through: (1) increased intra-abdominal pressure during apnea → increased venous return → ANP/BNP release → increased nocturnal urine production; (2) disrupted sleep architecture → decreased arousal to bladder distention.
